subtopic: DISCONTINUANCE OF DOMINION CONTRIBUTIONS- NORTHERN SASKATCHEWAN SETTLERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker. I had intended to ask a question of the Minister of Labour, but in his absence perhaps the Minister of Agriculture might answer.
In view of the fact that dominion contributions for relief to the provinces are being discontinued on March 31, what responsibility will the federal government take for supplying food to the northern settlers in Saskatchewan who are being reestablished under a joint dominion-provincial arrangement, in the event that the province cannot care for these settlers? What announcement, if any, has been made by the Saskatchewan government in connection with supplying relief after March 31?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: DISCONTINUANCE OF DOMINION CONTRIBUTIONS- NORTHERN SASKATCHEWAN SETTLERS
speechtext:
In the absence of the Minister of Labour I have been asked by him to reply as follows:-
It has always been the responsibility of the provincial or local authorities, acting under provincial regulation, to determine to whom, to what extent and under what conditions assistance is granted. The dominion responsibility was largely that of assisting the provinces financially. It is assumed that the provincial authorities will arrange to take care of those in need after March 31 without dominion assistance. I have no information as to the intention of the Saskatchewan government.

To provide for payments on reductions in wheat acreages, under conditions prescribed by the governor in council, for administration expenses in connection therewith, and for temporary appointments that may be required notwithstanding anything contained in the Civil Service Act, $35,000,000.

Mr. Chairman, I made a few remarks yesterday concerning the matter of procedure with respect to this item. I do not propose to repeat anything I said then. In my remarks to-day I shall review the criticisms of the government's proposals, and I hope to make a few constructive suggestions.
The wheat problem is not of recent origin; indeed it goes back to the years succeeding the last war, when the wheat-importing nations of Europe adopted the policy of attempting to become self-supporting communities.
If you will examine the record you will find that beginning with the year 1922, and in succeeding years down to at least 1934, the importing European countries, such as Germany and France, began by a succession of
rMr. J. A. MacKinnon.!
tariff increases, quota systems and other limitations, to cut down their imports of wheat until finally some of them, notably France, actually became exporters of wheat.
What was the reason for this? Frankly I think it was that they were afraid of war. They were afraid of the difficulties of transportation in time of war, but over and above all these reasons they were afraid of the price they had to pay for wheat during the great war. They determined that never again would they pay ransom to America for their bread.
Upon whom did this policy fall most heavily? Without doubt upon Canada, the United States and the Argentine, and upon Canada most of all. What did Canada do? Did she take cognizance of the growth of economic nationalism in Europe with respect to wheat? She did not-most emphatically she did not. During the time the right hon. gentleman and his party were in power and in control of government policy, this country increased its wheat acreage from 18 million acres in 1921 to over 25 million acres in 1930. Production in terms of bushels grew from 300 million bushels in 1921 to 479 million bushels in 1927, to 566 million bushels in 1929 and to 420 million bushels in 1930. In terms of dollars and cents the value of exports of wheat and wheat flour for the crop year 1925-26-the first year for which the figures have been made available to me-was $475 million, but in 1930-31 this had fallen to $188 million.
May I pause here to say that the problem first became acute at about this time, early in 1930. I really have never been able to make up my mind whether the then government, the then minister of agriculture, the then minister of finance, were aware of the situation rapidly coming to a head. But the evidence is that the government of my right hon. friend had not at the beginning of 1930 the slightest appreciation or understanding of the wheat problem then rapidly approaching. On February 20, 1930, the right hon. gentleman put these words into the mouth of his excellency in the speech from the throne:
The dominion is already recovering from the seasonal slackness evident at the end of the year and it is not to be forgotten that the bulk of the 1929 "wheat crop still remains in Canadian hands for final disposition.
Mr. Chairman, mark well that sentence! We, in common with the rest of the world, were then in the fourth month of the greatest economic depression the world had ever seen, and the right hon. gentleman called it a "seasonal slackness"! What vision! How characteristic of him! Trying the old game of lulling the Canadian people into a sense of false security. And then how naive the

statement that "the bulk of the 1929 wheat crop still remains in Canadian hands for final disposition"!
That was the position with respect to wheat which the Bennett government inherited in 1930. The crop of 1929 still remained unsold in the hands of the farmers. The problem continued down through the years to 1935, and then the Bennett government had to take over the whole burden and establish a new policy.
In the meantime marketing prices went from bad to worse. Wheat went down in price in 1933 on the world's markets to the lowest price in 400 years. The selling agency of the pools had called in John I. McFarland in 1930 to take over the problem. The government in the course of time had to put the credit of the country behind the agency, and it did so. This action carried the situation through to 1935, and no matter what the criticism was, the fact is that the operations of John I. McFarland never cost Canada one cent. On the contrary in the final accounting the McFarland operations resulted in a substantial profit to the treasury, and it should have been far more than it was.
I want to pause here to pay a tribute to Mr. McFarland. He was not employed by the government. He was employed by the pools, and he undertook, without salary, to serve Canada, and particularly western Canada, to the best of his ability-an ability, I believe, without a peer in that particular field. He gave himself so unremittingly to the task that I believe his health was permanently impaired. But what 'he did, he did for Canada, and I am sure the farmers of western Canada, irrespective of party politics, respect him and look upon him to-day as one of the greatest friends western agriculture ever had.
Then in the session of 1935 the government took, in the face of the sternest opposition from gentlemen opposite and from the trade, the only possible constructive position that was open to it. It decided on the establishment of the wheat board.
Hon. gentlemen who aTe interested in the position at that time may read with a good deal of profit Mr. Bennett's speech on the second reading of the bill on June 12, 1935, in which he traced the history of the production and sale of wheat in the whole world and its relation to Canada, and in which he made a most reasoned argument in support of the measure.
The terms of the 1935 bill were simple. It provided for the marketing of Canada's wheat crop through a government board, not through private enterprise. Why? In the
circumstances private enterprise had failed, and it has failed ever since. That was the fundamental reason. Nobody wanted to put the government into the wheat business, but because there was no other method, no other agency that would function, the wheat board was established. Another reason was that a wheat board would ensure against the destruction of that measure of economic stability which had been built up in the most trying years of the history of wheat production in Canada. The bill was offered on the further theory that Canada had an obligation not only to herself, as the chief exporter and the third greatest producer of wheat, but also to the other wheat exporting countries, to give such help and assistance as we were able, to prevent wheat from being sold at prices ruinous to the producers. Generally speaking, these were the principles upon which that legislation was based.	.
The advent of another great world war has accentuated the position. It has not changed, except in degree, the underlying position.
May I pause here now to examine the position of hon. gentlemen opposite, who were then sitting on this side. I well remember it. They were hostile to the principle. Who was their spokesman? He was the same gentleman who is now Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston). At page 3581 of Hansard of 1935 he made this statement:
I do not believe that the people of the Dominion of Canada are favourable to a compulsory wheat board-
Well, we have it; we have it to-day.
-to a board the constitution of which will mean that every wheat grower, every elevator man and everybody engaged in the business must deal with the government agency and no one else.
That was the attitude of my hon. friend in 1935. But while he gave expression to that view, he did not venture to challenge the measure. He was afraid to strike. Discretion was the better part of valour with him and his colleagues. He left us with the impression that while he would like to kill the bill he dared not do so. No wonder that at the conclusion of his speech one hon. gentleman asked him if he was for or against the bill. No one knew.
The board was set up in 1935. The election came. The Bennett government was defeated. The members of the board were dismissed and new men were appointed in their place. Was the personnel improved? That is a question which I leave to the people of Canada to answer. The essential point is that the principle of government control of the wheat business was maintained, and for definite and good reasons.

I shall not follow the operations of the board from 1935 down to 1938, but I do assert that the marketing of the 1938 crop gave the Canadian Wheat Board Act its first real chance to function. Canada faced the crop year 1938-39 with empty granaries. The world carryover was 40 per cent below the previous five-year average. Early in that crop year, in August, 1938, cash wheat was around 85 cents at Winnipeg and October futures, 75 cents. That year the world acreage sown to wheat was exceptionally large and a heavy crop resulted.
The exporting countries had available for export around 1,200,000,000 bushels, including the small carryover, and we in Canada had available for export approximately 50 per cent of the needs of the importing countries, including Britain. This was not an inviting marketing condition; on the contrary, it was a most uninviting condition.
The initial price of No. 1 northern was fixed at 80 cents by the federal cabinet under the authority of the Canadian Wheat Board Act, and this formed the basis for fixed prices for other grades of wheat. This minimum price was accepted by the cabinet upon the recommendation of the wheat board. The price was announced by the Prime Minister on the evening of August 4, 1938, and on that occasion he made the following general statement:
The policy of the Canadian wheat board will not be to hoard wheat, nor to speculate upon it, nor to seek to establish a monopoly. Canadian wheat will be moved promptly to market.
The announcement went on to state that the minimum price had been accepted by the cabinet upon the recommendation of the Canadian wheat board, and therefore both the cabinet and the wheat board were responsible for the position.
It was evident from the Prime Minister's remarks that the fixing of the 80-cent price was a form of compensating adjustment for the western farmer, who had suffered greatly in recent years because of drought and crop failures. At the same time, the Prime Minister released an announcement from the Hon. W. D. Euler, then Minister of Trade and Commerce, to the effect that Canadian wheat would be competing in world markets; and the milling and grain trades of the world were advised that, notwithstanding the internal initial price of 80 cents a bushel, the Canadian wheat board would continue its work of encouraging the use of Canadian wheat-and now, Mr. Chairman, mark these words-"which will at all times be competitive on the world's markets."

Then things began to happen. There were immediate reactions to the statement of the Prime Minister and the announcement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. In the United States it was announced that 100 million bushels would be dumped on the world's markets. The Argentine gave its president discretionary powers to fix a margin between domestic and export prices. Australia and other exporting countries acted in response; and all the importing countries except Britain tightened up restrictions, some to the point of exclusion.
Now mark this! In less than one month after Canada's official announcement of the price was made and after the announcement attributed to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that, notwithstanding the initial price of 80 cents a bushel, Canadian wheat would be competing in world markets and that the wheat board would continue its work of encouraging the use of Canadian wheat, which would at all times be competitive on the world markets, the cash prices and price of futures at Winnipeg went down to below 60 cents a bushel.
The government's announcement resulted in sev ere damage to Canadian wheat prices. There was an immediate cash loss of $52,000,000 to the treasury. That $52,000,000 was a contribution which had been advanced by the treasury to the wheat board. An ultimate total deficit of $61,282,329.55 on the wheat crop of 1938-39 resulted. There is no question about this ultimate loss. It is admitted in exhibit B attached to the Canadian wheat board report of the crop year 1939-40, dated January 11, 1941, which recently came into our hands.
These are the facts. These results are not to be dismissed as a mere error of judgment. They are the natural result flowing from the policy announced by the government that Canadian wheat would at all times be competitive on the world markets. The fixing of the minimum price at SO cents was government policy', not a mere leap in the dark; the fall in price in the world markets was a direct result of the announcement of the then Minister of Trade and Commerce. It meant that, while the price had been fixed at 80 cents, yet the wheat would be sold at world prices, to whatever level they' might fall. What a situation in a buyers' market!
This considered policy of the government is not to be regarded as a mere error of judgment, or ineptitude in the transaction of public business. The invitation was made to world buyers not to take the 80-cent price as a minimum; it was an invitation to world buyers, in a buyers' market, to hammer the

price downward, and this invitation was accepted with alacrity and with the results already noted.
As a result of the fall in prices invited by this government, the wheat board failed to sell the 1938-39 crop, and the failure to sell that crop was the primary cause of the debacle in the wheat situation in Canada-not the declaration of war in September, 1939.
It has been said by a cynic that, "as wheat marketers, governments and parliaments have more money than brains, and they are poor substitutes for private trading." Be that as it may, the government and the wheat board proceeded on the theory of a double market, that is to say, government regimentation on the one hand and competitive marketing on the other, at a time when the world wheat market was a buyers' market. That theory was a defiance of the law of supply and demand and of the principles of mathematics.
Notwithstanding the tremendous loss to the treasury of Canada which ensued from this policy, one lesson ought to have emerged, and that is-and I state this very plainly and succinctly-that the treasury of Canada cannot be placed behind unlimited production of wheat. To do so is to invite disaster for all concerned.
After this debacle of 1938-39 came the war. It served to intensify the problem.
Last year, 1940, we had not a policy but an improvisation-the quota system of deliveries -and the levy of the processing tax on domestic consumption. The quota system has probably worked out better than was anticipated, because the quota was enlarged. One thing, however, has emerged. It has transferred to the Canadian people the ownership of the greatest volume of wheat in the history of the country, involving an investment in unsaleable wheat of between $400 and S500 millions, at a time when the Canadian people are being asked to raise, by way of taxation and loan, a sum which will fall not far short of $3,000 million. What a staggering load for twelve million people!
Early in the present session of parliament, on November 14 last, to be exact, the Minister of Agriculture, following his return from Britain, made a speech in this house by way of a report on his visit, in which speech he dealt with wheat and during the course of which he did some prophesying-a very dangerous procedure. If his prophecy was correct, then there is no cause for agony or alarm on the part of either the producers or the taxpayers. If he was right, there is nothing to worry about.

I suggest that this is not the kind of stuff that the Canadian people should be fed with by a responsible minister of the crown. I do not think anyone will be deceived by it, least of all the producers. Certainly it will not deceive the taxpayers of Canada. It is on a par with the propaganda we heard all last summer and autumn with regard to Canada's war effort, which propaganda happily is to be abandoned, so at least says my hon. friend the Minister of Munitions and Supply. He said he was not going to make any more prophecies, which I think is wise.
The Minister of Agriculture even ventured into the field of finance. He told us his plan would mean that the government would require to foot a total of $620,000,000. I suggest to him-it is a matter of opinion-[DOT] that he is not very realistic. In less than a year we are involved to the tune of $400 million or more invested in wheat. We have not the amount that must be added in respect of bank loans and carrying charges, but we are being invited to go much further in the bonusing programme, in wheat storage, in subsidies under the two-year depreciation plan, and in the actual investment in wheat. If this goes on the Canadian people with respect to wheat may well visualize through treasury commitments, interest, carrying charges, loss of income taxation through the depreciation allowance and so on, a total of well up to a billion dollars. It may actually come to that. My guess is as good as the minister's.

speechtext: It is a well known rule of the house that when an hon. gentleman has the floor no one can interrupt him without his leave; but this rule has been honoured more in the breach than in the observance, and a good deal of latitude has been given by the Chair even to the present speaker. I would point out, however, that this may once more exemplify the desirability of always observing the rule, and perhaps the leader of the opposition, who now has the floor and who has experienced what interruptions by other speakers mean, will give an example to the whole house. My task in the committee of the whole has been difficult. I have tried to apply the rules, but in a human way, allowing some latitude. I shall continue to do so, but I would observe to all hon. members that it is best to follow the rules at all times, because they are based upon experience and wisdom.

Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman. I have no great objection to interruptions. What I really do object to is the chatter that of course is intended to throw one off one's train of thought. I do not think that is quite cricket. The minister says he cannot help interrupting me because I am looking at him. That is
the most natural thing in the world; he is directly in front of me, and in a measure I am really talking to him as well as to the government. However, this little interlude will do no harm to any of us.
Now I turn to another topic. The government's policy for the current year was announced on March 12 by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture, after many delays and much hesitation, and I think I am safe in saying that it does not please anyone. However, it is just another improvised policy, not intended to be permanent, for which I think most of us are grateful.
I rather compliment the Minister of Trade and Commerce on having made a factual statement comparatively free from propaganda and containing a good deal of information. He dealt with the quota system, the plan of payment for farm storage, deliveries, disposition of the carryover, the storage situation and allied questions.
With respect to the crop situation for 1941-42 he gave us an authoritative statement that the carryover will amount to 575 million bushels. Then he added a prophecy based on an average of say 425,000,000 bushels for the new crop, which would produce a total of 1,000 million bushels. I suggest that this is a supply never before reached in the history of Canada, or even contemplated. It is a situation calculated to make the bravest among us pause and reflect. It is a supply away beyond the storage capacity of this country.
In addition to this, hon. gentlemen must visualize a further difficulty, namely, the carryover of 400 million bushels in the United States. In the present world position that is a factor we cannot leave out of consideration. On the basis of expectation only, we are to consume in Canada for domestic and other purposes 127 million bushels, and we may export 180 million, or a total expected disappearance of 307 million bushels. I suggest that this outlook is optimistic; it is not likely to be reached, though it may be. Therefore we will have a carryover of more than
700,000,000 bushels, an all-time high.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce stressed lightly the financial position, though he admitted that it called for anxiety. A loss of $67,000,000 on 1938-39 and 1939-40 operations is a staggering sum, but as I pointed out before this figure does not include interest on bank balances on the 1938 crop, or carrying charges on the 1939 crop since July 31 last, both of which must be substantial and should have been included to get a correct appreciation of the position.

Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner):	The
one is complementary to the other; the two, read together, constitute the policy.
What is his proposal? In brief it is that the wheat farmer is to be bonused-for the first time in Canadian history-not to produce. That is the outstanding feature of the minister's policy. The minister, through his staff of inspectors, and what not, is to have up to $35 million to play with-and probably more. I wonder if hon. members understand the implications of the minister's words yesterday when he talked about warrants. I have just looked up the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act. I can visualize that if this is not enough the minister is going back to council -to the treasury board first, and then to council-with a recommendation. This may go to $75 million, or more. In any event I suggest the whole proposition is objectionable. An army of inspectors will be appointed, and the whole position may degenerate into a racket.
Its immediate reaction on me is that it is a clumsy and belated effort to imitate one of the earlier policies of Mr. Henry A. Wallace as part of the new deal in the United States. The reaction to the entire proposal is disappointing, alike to the producers themselves, who will suffer from insufficient farm income, and to the taxpayers, who will have to foot the bills.

As to certain considerations and features which stand out prominently, we will all be in agreement:-
1.	It is known that the government cannot dispose of all the wheat grown, and therefore cannot be expected to buy it. I think we all agree on that.
2.	Since the government is in the wheat business, and since the quota system is recognized, I ask myself this question: Why should not the price be a fair price? That is to say, why should it not be a price comparable with that of cheese, bacon and other farm products?
3.	The wheat business is the most controlled business in Canada and the law of supply and demand is entirely suspended. Therefore why not pay a price at least equivalent to the cost of production?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: What would you make it?

I do not know; but I would have it investigated by those who do know. Why should I set myself up as an expert and say that 75 cents, 85 cents, 80 cents, or 90 cents, is the cost of production? It would be foolish for me to attempt to do that. But there are those who do know and, as a matter of fact, the cost of production can be established. I am contending for a principle, that is all. I suggest the price should not be above the levels of other farm products, but since its marketing and disposition is in the absolute control of the federal government there is no real reason why the price paid for the wheat taken should not be a fair one.
4.	I believe it would be a much better policy-at least it would be better for the producers themselves-if the government were to pay what it would consider fair for such wheat as it can take and dispose of, and leave to the farmer the task and responsibility of doing his own planning. Now he is regimented both going and coming, and, to make the dose more palatable, he is to be paid for non-producing.
Recently I read the opinion of the president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. He said at Hamilton on March 15, as reported by the Canadian Press, that the federal government's wheat policy will work hardships on both western and eastern Canadian farmers. He described the policy as "one of those double-barrelled shot-gun affairs, which soaked the western farmer by leaving the minimum price for a limited quota at the

Supply-Agriculture-Wheat Acreages
depression figure of 70 cents a bushel" and "soaked the eastern farmer by paying western farmers to intensify competition in the staple products of eastern agriculture." Mr. Hannam went on to say:
The new programme is a good example of the folly of trying to carry on without a national agricultural marketing and production programme.
He argued further-and consideration ought to be given by the government to this suggestion-that:
. . . the swing of nine million acres out of wheat into other products in one sudden swoop is something which should have been accomplished by a crop adjustment programme spread over at least a three-year period.
It should have been started a year ago. Any thoughtful person will, I suggest, agree with him. Finally he condemned the whole scheme and threw it out of the window by saying:
The lack of an adequate farm policy for the dominion means that agriculture becomes the victim of a series of ill-advised last-minute emergency measures which cannot be regarded in even our most generous moments as the product of competent leadership or good statesmanship.
That is an indictment. I believe it will be the considered opinion of all those who study this problem that the government's proposals are ill-advised last-minute emergency measures which are the product of incompetent leadership and lack of statesmanship.
Already the minister has heard mumblings of discontent. It will not be surprising if before this debate ends the whole scheme will be changed. I believe the minister has already given some indication that he has heard from both the east and. the west.
I had intended to examine what was asked by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture through its delegation which met the government as long ago as January 27, 1941. I shall not, however, take time to go into this matter in detail. They made a very patriotic declaration with respect to agriculture in Canada, stating that-
Canadian agriculture's first task and .paramount duty is to place its whole strength and unite its resources from sea to sea behind Canada's war effort.
I believe that is the attitude of our farmers; I have no doubt about it. They said further:
The war must be won, and the greatest possible degree of national unity is essential if our war effort is to reach maximum efficiency.
To state that is to state the truth.
Then they proceeded to declare that victory cannot be achieved without sacrifice-a point I have emphasized on many occasions. "All classes of our people," they say, "will 14873-124
be called upon to make sacrifices, and the agricultural industry is ready and willing to bear its full share of the heavy load which Canada has shouldered."
The federation went on to declare:
It is vital, from considerations of national unity, that no one class shall be called upon to carry an undue share of the burden, and that there should be equality of sacrifice by all classes.
I stand four-square behind that declaration. There must be equality of sacrifice. Who is making the greatest sacrifice in Canada to-day? The producer of primary products. I have always noted to my dismay that in time of depression the first prices to fall and the last to rise are the prices of primary products. This is a striking indictment of our present system, of the capitalist system, if you will. I have no panacea to offer at the moment, but I do say that this problem is a challenge to the best brains and the best statesmanship in the world, which ought to be brought to bear upon it to find, if at all possible, a solution.
The brief went on to declare the importance of the agricultural industry in terms of the numbers engaged in it, and then dealt with the question of the distribution of the national income. Everyone has read this. To me it is appalling that with the national income rising as rapidly as our friends say it is-I know it is rising very rapidly but I doubt whether it is rising as rapidly as it is said to be by the statisticians-the share of the national income accruing to the average primary producer should be so pitifully small.
The brief went on to speak of the whole agricultural picture. That I shall not repeat here. But I do want to refer to the brief's recommendations with respect to wheat, with some of which I agree and with some of which I disagree.
First of all it recommended that a compulsory restriction of the acreage seeded to wheat would be undesirable at the present time. I agree with that, provided the restriction was confined to Canada. An attempt was made in the last decade to limit world wheat acreage, and if that could have been undertaken as an international activity it would have been the very best thing that could have been done. But it failed. I am not going to place the responsibility on anyone, although we all know what happened in 1933. The attempt failed because you could not get international action. It is of no use to ask the Canadian agriculturist to reduce his acreage while extending an invitation to the Argentine and other wheat producing countries to increase their acreage. That is not the right way to go about it, nor could it be productive of any beneficial results.

But I do say this: upon giving the farmers fair notice that the government can take delivery of only so much wheat, you could have trusted the farmers themselves to do their own planning over a period of time and adjust their acreage sown to wheat. They would be likely to do it. The intelligent ones would do it, and the others would follow suit. If farmers know they are not likely to market their wheat they will not sow so much.
The second recommendation was that the wheat board should undertake to announce the total amount of wheat of which it is prepared to accept delivery.
That has been done, and I think it was the proper thing for the board to make that announcement. Certainly it could not accept the whole production of our Canadian wheat fields, because the public treasury, other things considered, could not stand it. I think therefore the government has been wise in announcing the total amount of wheat that it will take. Some people believe that the amount is not large enough, but I leave that question to those who are better informed than I am. The underlying principle is sound, and I commend the minister for that.
Another recommendation called for an increase in the initial payment for wheat delivered in the crop year 1941. That has been refused.
I draw attention to the next recommendation, and I face fairly and squarely the question raised thereby. They asked for a processing tax of not less than 50 cents a bushel. The recommendation reads:
That a processing tax of not less than 50 cents per bushel should be placed on all wheat milled for domestic consumption, the tax to be added to the aggregate price received for the wheat marketed and be available for the purpose of increasing the initial payment to the farmer.
That has been refused, in my judgment properly so; because to grant it would furnish an added incentive to farmers not to cut down the acreage sown to wheat but to go on and produce in the hope that through pressure the government would ultimately take the wheat, thereby adding to the burdens of the country. Notwithstanding what the member for Qu'Appelle has said about the price of bread, I have no doubt that a processing tax of 50 cents a bushel would add to the price of bread.
Why should it?
I am sure it would.
There is no reason for it.

I am not
going to work out the mathematics of it now,

but I believe that it would increase the price of bread just as surely as I believe that I am standing on my two feet.
The fifth recommendation related to grain storage facilities, and in this regard stress was laid on the need of a reserve for a constant supply of wheat to Great Britain in the event of possible crop failure during the war and for the needs of the people of Europe when the war was won. The specific recommendation was that the dominion government be asked to provide financial assistance to farmers for the construction of adequate farm storage facilities to enable the farmer to adjust his deliveries.
That recommendation was ignored. I believe that it is perfectly feasible, at least from the standpoint of legality. I know there is fear that you could not police this wheat on the farm, but that difficulty could be overcome. Personally I think, as the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) argued last night, that the farmer should be encouraged to establish and maintain on his farm adequate storage facilities so that he might reap the benefit of the charges that accrue from that class of storage. I ask the minister to reconsider that part of his proposals.

speechtext: If I might be permitted, I said in my speech yesterday that this was one of the questions that could not properly be determined until about July of this year.

I quite
appreciate that the minister said that, and if he is looking for a pat on the back he is getting it right now. My friend from the west behind me says that there may not be any wheat to be carried over. I hope he is right.
I hope he is wrong. I hope we have a crop.

Perhaps
I did not understand the implication of his interjection. I certainly hope there will be a crop and that storage facilities will be provided so that not one kernel of wheat will be destroyed. It is all going to be needed some time, and the only problem is how to carry it in the meantime.

May I direct the attention of the house and the country to the manner in which the government has dealt with the question of providing new storage facilities.
This problem was discussed at great length at the last session, when the amendments to the wheat board act were before the house in late July and early August. At that time the government intimated that discussions were being carried on with the elevator companies with respect to increased storage. They were at that time I think opposed to the giving of financial aid to increase farm storage. We were unable to get any information at the close of the session.
After the house rose in August, arrangements were made with the elevator companies to provide for what is termed temporary storage at the elevators in the country. These new erections, being additions to country elevators, were built by these companies without any order in council having been passed, so far as I can ascertain, but, as I understand it, upon a ruling by the income tax branch that the costs could be written off in two years and absorbed in depreciation account. I tried to look into the legality of this position, and apparently it is based upon paragraph (n) of section 6 of the Income War Tax Act, which leaves the power to determine depreciation allowance in the uncontrolled discretion of the minister:
6.	In computing the amount of the profits or gains to be assessed, a deduction shall not be allowed in respect of
(n) depreciation, except such amount as the minister in his discretion may allow, including such extra depreciation as the minister in his discretion may allow in the case of plant and equipment built or acquired to fulfil orders for war purposes.
A ruling was given by the commissioner of income tax on August 6, 1940, covering the so-called balloon annexes, from which ruling I quote in part:
It has been determined that the capital expenditures to erect temporary or "balloon" annexes will be written off out of gross revenue in two years, namely, 1940 and 1941.
This would appear to me to have been a most liberal arrangement. I have been advised-this is hearsay evidence, not the best evidence by any means-that in many instances these structures will be good for from five to ten years. At all events they will be good for the probable duration of the war. The benefit of the allowance will enure entirely to the elevator companies who, notwithstanding the limited turnover and the slight reduction in storage charges, are enjoying capacity business and probably, in their capacity as warehousemen, making more money than at any time in their history.

In fact, it may be stated that our elevator companies are the only people who are benefiting by the present situation. A perusal of the balance sheets of those companies which publish balance sheets will indicate this. Why should the government not review this position? Is it not the consensus of opinion that under present circumstances the storage charges are too high, having regard to the capacity business being done?
Then on February 15, 1941, order in council P.C. 1225 was passed providing for assistance by way of depreciation allowance for income tax purposes to any elevator operating company which constructs temporary terminal storage at the head of the lakes. That is a most generous gesture to the elevator trade. No part of the benefit accruing to these companies by this assistance accrues to the producer or to the grain trade, unless it be that the grain trade and elevator companies are intermingled by ownership and that sort of thing. Recently the plight of the members of the grain trade was brought to my attention. The plight of those who are not interested in the elevator business is a sad one. The Winnipeg grain exchange was kept open by the government it is said at the request of the British authorities. I am informed, however, that the Liverpool exchange and the British market are closed to-day. I have not been able to verify this, but that is the information which comes to me from the grain trade. I ask the minister: why has the Winnipeg grain exchange been kept open? what useful function can it perform when there is only one buyer and only one seller?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The reason was given to the house last year, namely, that the British cereals board asked us to keep it open.
That is the government's stock answer.
Who represents that board in Winnipeg?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I do not know that anyone represents it in Winnipeg.

I might offer another
reason. Wheat is the only article controlled by the wheat board under any legislation, but we have considerable quantities of other cereals such as rye, oats and barley, which are sold. It is necessary to have a market for them.

It may be that that is a satisfactory reason. At the moment I am viewing the matter only from the point of view of wheat.
Facilities good for a much longer period are to be paid for out of depreciation allowance in two years, and this for companies already

doing well financially out of the grain trade. The effect of this is a substantial bonus to the terminal elevator companies, and I have heard that they are taking advantage of this with great alacrity.
I wish to deal briefly with the bonus question. What of the policy of the bonus? Is this the minister's own policy? He told us last night that it was the joint policy of the government. We have all heard the principle of -cabinet solidarity, but I am just wondering whether if the minister were left on -his own resources, he would have brought in this bonus policy. I have the idea that it is the joint product of the government's brain trust. I should like to be informed if that is true, because it sma-cks of the new deal in the United States, a throw-back to the discarded policies of Mr. Wallace, a clumsy and belated imitation.
The whole wheat policy was received in the west with surprise and dismay, or so say the pools, and they claim to represent the producers. The producer knows his own land. He knows it is useless to produce if he cannot sell; that is, provided he has a level head upon his shoulders. He naturally will plan his own economy. The large producer will do his own planning, because he knows. But what of the small producer on a half-section or less? How will it -affect him? What hope has he unde-r this policy? The relatively small amount which each small farmer will be able to market, the increased cost of operation, production and living, and the fact that seventy cents is less -than to-day's production cost, make the proposed plan wholly inadequate.
Stated concisely in a nutshell, the western wheat farmer is being asked, because of limited deliveries, without any increase in price, to accept a sharp reduction in farm income from wheat. Deducting freight rates and handling charges the seventy cent basic price for No. 1 northern at Fort William is equivalent to less than fifty cents on the average prairie farm. I am told that it is equivalent to only forty-eight cents. The sale of 230 million bushels will net these farmers $115,000,000, the lowest income from this source since 1933. This is just about h-alf the value of wheat marketings during the present crop year. It will be really less than -that, because that price is the maximum that may be hoped for. How can the western wheat farmer live on an income which is less than two-thirds of last year's income. By this bonus of $36,000,000? Assuredly not.
What are the alternatives? They appear to me to be two:

1.	An increase in taxation passed along to the consumer by way of a processing or some allied tax.
2.	An increase in the basic price of wheat.
I have said before that in my opinion an
increase in the processing tax cannot be justified. At best, it was only a makeshift, designed to reduce the loss to the treasury. It was never designed to aid the farmer in the initial price he was to get. It was to reduce the deficit. To increase it to 50 cents would mean a tax on bread, and in the interests of the consumer that should be definitely barred. Its retention at 15 cents is an expedient, it is true, but refusal to increase it is a declaration of policy on the part of the government not to expand further this form of taxation. Definitely it is a tax which falls with unequal weight upon the lower income groups. It is in the -class of regressive taxation of a particularly undesirable kind. We should get rid of it just as quickly as possible. To raise it would increase the cost of living, upon which would be based a justifiable demand for higher wages, thus setting in motion all the inflationary forces so difficult to control in time of war-forces which, I fear, are already in operation.
What is the only other alternative? The only alternative I can see is this-and I offer this to the committee and the countiy for what it is worth. I hope that hon. gentlemen in discussing it will not deprecate the source from which it comes, because it is an honest expression of opinion based upon the best information I can get from my friends in the western country, who at least know something about wheat. The only alternative is to raise the basic price to the farmer to a point which would at least approach cost of production, and approach parity with prices of other farm products and prices which the farmer has to pay for the implements of production and maintenance of a decent standard of living.
Such a policy is justifiable if the farmer is to keep body and soul together and remain on the land. That is something that we -have all been trying to do down through the years of development of this country. In all parts of Canada we have sought at great cost to keep the farmer on the land. We are not abandoning that policy, I hope, and I advocate this even if such higher price involves some additional taxation; and if additional taxation is necessaiy for that purpose, there are more equitable ways of raising it -than by an increase in the processing tax.
The bonus in theory is a compensating measure which will fail in its objective. It is negative in all its attributes and will please

Supply-Agriculture-Wheat Acreages
no one. The big farmer in existing circumstances will, I am told, summer-fallow anyway. He is to be paid now for doing that which his judgment tells him he should do under present circumstances. I have heard of a farmer in the west who had definitely decided to summer-fallow 750 acres of land this year which was in wheat last year. He will still do it and will be paid $3,000 for doing it.
Who was that?

That is my secret. The small farmer of a half-section or less-how can he exist on the theory of this bonus? Most of them will turn to coarse grain and a $2 bonus, and go into hogs. We heard about that last night from Ontario members, and we shall hear more about it before the item passes. Then with his cheaper feed, think of the competition of these people with the farmers of eastern Canada. The latter will have no bonus. In the maritimes we have a good many hog raisers, and we are finding it exceedingly difficult to compete with the Ontario farmer because of the high cost of mill feed. I am bound to say this, that the Minister of Agriculture offered to cooperate with the provincial governments of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, paying half the freight from Fort William, and he could not get his friends down there to accept his offer. I do not understand why, if they were giving consideration to the hog raisers of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, the minister's offer was not accepted. At least, it was a half-way measure. But they did not accept it and there the matter stands. So far as I know, they have never given publicly any reason why they refused that offer. I suppose the idea is that if they waited and pressed long enough, the dominion government would go the whole way. That is the theory in the minds of some people. They forget entirely that while there are nine or ten public treasuries in Canada, there is only one set of taxpayers.
There are just one or two other aspects upon which I should like to touch. I apologize for keeping the committee so long, but this is my contribution to this debate, and perhaps it may add something to the sum total of the knowledge of the house and of the country.
We are all exceedingly grateful for the lease-lend bill recently passed by the congress of the United States. It may well be that the aid and support to Britain given under that measure will be the turning point in the war. Indeed, I think it will be and I am extremely grateful for it. But I wonder whether-and I am not saying this in any attempt to throw any doubt on the validity of their desire to help-as a matter of economic
fact, the government and hon. gentlemen in this house have considered that the aid to be given and given freely by the United States is not to be confined to war material and to equipment. It may and undoubtedly will in time take the form of gifts of supplies -food supplies. Indeed, already they are planning to send wheat and wheat flour to unoccupied France. Undoubtedly they will be giving wheat and wheat flour to the mother country. Has the government visualized that? I wonder what our reaction will be to that. We cannot say nay. My immediate reaction is that it will just add to our troubles. I do not see any other way out of it. You cannot ask the British government to refuse it. The offer would indicate a very fine disposition on the part of the people of the United States.
May I recall to the minds of hon. gentlemen that on July 10 last I asked this government to give consideration to the idea of an outright gift of 100,000,000 bushels of wheat to the mother country. It would not help the price; it would not help the storage position much, but it would be a great gesture to the hard-pressed people of Britain. Any one who cares to look it up can see what I said. I am bound to say, however, that it brought not a ripple of response from this government and I have often wondered why. Is it that we are doing so much otherwise? We are. of course; but I have always thought that Canada, out of her great abundance, not as an expedient but as a gesture of good will and of admiration, could give to the people of the mother country some of our superabundance of wheat. The people of the United States are contributing to-day, as a trial shipment, a million dollars' worth of flour to the people ot unoccupied France. It is a trial shipment, and if it goes through and does not get into the hands of Germany, others will follow. Canada undoubtedly will in time be asked to make some contribution in food to the starving peoples of Europe. How much the more should we do that for the hard-pressed people of Britain who find it so hard to get Canadian dollars? I here and now renew my suggestion to the Canadian government and ask them out of the billion and a half dollars which they are asking the Canadian people to raise under *the war appropriation bill to give some of our abundance to our kith and kin across the ocean.
On Tuesday last, the Prime Minister took occasion to point with pride to the contribution of the Canadian people-not the government, he laid emphasis on that, but the Canadian people-to Britain's war effort in terms of our armed forces, equipment and,

I do not intend to follow the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) through all his arguments both for and against himself on this question, but I shall touch on one or two things that he said.
In the first place he spoke of the amount of wheat Canada had on hand on account of the operations of John I. McFarland. We did have a great deal of wheat on hand when this government first came into office, and the main reason for that immense stock was that we would not sell. After Mr. Murray took over the chairmanship of the wheat board the policy put into effect was to sell wheat on the British market and other markets. At that time, when that policy was put into effect, the mix of Canadian wheat in the mills of Great Britain was only about seven per cent of the total. As a result of this policy Canadian wheat was sold, and that mix has gone up to seventy per cent in British flour, and that figure holds there to-day.
I agree with some of the things my hon. friend said. He did not make much reference to the last war, but wheat, and especially Canadian wheat, was a very important factor in the winning of that war. We in the west who were wheat farmers at that time were asked by the government of this country to extend greatly our acreage in order that Great Britain and our allies might have sufficient food. Wheat was badly needed before that war was over, it will be badly needed again before this war is over. Never in the world's history has there been a war in which foodstuffs, of which wheat is the most important, were not badly needed before the finish and immediately thereafter.
But, as my hon. friend has said, preparations for the present conflict began long before September, 1939, and it was because of this war economy that the world business of growing and selling wheat was disrupted. It was the war economy which was developing for years prior to September, 1939, that dislocated the whole wheat business of the world, and our people suffered on that account. In September, 1939, actual hostilities started, and thereafter wheat began to rise in price. Many people have asked me why the western farmer sowed more wheat acreage last spring when he knew the initial price of wheat was only seventy cents. Last spring when the

western farmer was sowing wheat the price was ninety cents a bushel and over. That was before the low countries were invaded and before France was overrun. Everyone who knew anything about wheat at that time knew that if France were able to stay as an ally of Great Britain and to keep her country largely intact, at least 100 million bushels of wheat would have to be forwarded to France immediately. Italy was not in the war when we were sowing wheat last year, and it was reasonable to expect last spring that the price would rise, not fall.
Some hon. members have said that wheat is not a casualty of the war. It is. The price did not fall until after the low countries were invaded, until after France was being overrun and Italy stabbed her in the back. No one knew exactly at that time what was going to happen. No one knows now exactly what will happen within the next year.
Many people say that we should reduce our wheat acreage in this country. I do not altogether agree with that. I believe all the wheat we can produce from now until the end of this war will be needed, and needed badly. Nobody knows what devastation there will be this coming summer, both in Great Britain and in Europe, when crops are about to be harvested. Does anyone seriously think that both Great Britain and Germany, who are trying to carry out against each other a blockade of all foodstuffs, are going to stand by and let crops be harvested this summer and fall? I do not believe it. I believe the greatest devastation will occur in Europe this year. Incendiaries will be dropped in the fields where they cannot be fired at by antiaircraft guns, and great areas of farm crops will be burnt in all the countries affected. Wheat may be very badly needed by Great Britain and by our other allies before very long.
When the war started, and even last year, we did not have the allies fighting with us that we have to-day. Greece has come in since, and it looks very much as if Turkey will also come in. Yugoslavia has made a move-and remember that they are Serbs; it is springtime in Europe and the bear comes out in the spring. I will not be surprised if "the bear that walks like a man" is an ally of ours before very long, and also badly in need of wheat. No one can tell just what the situation will be; no one can tell how much wheat we shall be able to sell, even within the next year.
At the present time we as western members are asked to vote for a policy which, on its face, on the basis of last year's crop and last year's return, would seem to mean that our

wheat growers may have to take a reduction of some thirty per cent in their gross return.
I have heard arguments in this house from all sides in regard to the small farmer and how this policy will affect him, and in regard to the large farmer and how it will affect him. No one can tell how this policy will affect anyone. It is not the gross return to the farmer that must be taken into consideration. He is the same as any business man; it is the net return that you have to consider. If there should be an abundant crop in western Canada next year then. I would say that under this policy the net return to the farmer would be smaller. But if there should be a small average yield in western Canada next year I believe the net return to the farmer, large or small, would be better than if this policy were not in effect.
This government very properly called in experts in regard to wheat and the growing of grain, in order to obtain their advice as to what should be done. Then, naturally, they took what they thought to be the best advice of those experts. Well, Mr. Chairman, it is a little more than thirty years ago since I started growing wheat on my own farm in western Canada. During that time I have followed the wheat market pretty closely. I have known a good many of the grain men and grain experts; and if those experts have told the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the wheat committee of the cabinet that a long range policy should be one under which the acreage of wheat would be reduced; if they have told the committee that in the long run we can sell only so much wheat, I would tell the government that of one thing I am sure, and that is that the experts are one hundred per cent wrong. In all my experience I have never seen them right when they unanimously agreed on anything.
I want to warn the government against another wheat expert, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle.
You need not warn them.

The hon. gentleman sets himself up as a wheat expert in this country. I know he has had a good deal of experience; probably he has lost as much money as anyone still in the wheat business. Then we have the hon. member for Weyburn, to whom I listened very carefully yesterday in what I thought was a very moderate speech. The hon. gentleman made some suggestions which I considered were not too well thought out. For instance, he suggested that a farmer should be allowed to deliver from 750 to 1,000 bushels, at an increased price, on each quarter section of land.

On the first
quarter section, not each quarter section.
All right. There are 290,000 farmers-

Not wheat
farmers. There are 250,000 wheat farmers.

They would all
be wheat farmers if they could get a good price. If we allowed each of the 290,000 farmers in western Canada to deliver 1,000 bushels, that would mean an increased price on 290,000,000 bushels. On many occasions in this house I have listened with a good deal of interest to the hon. member speak about farming, -wheat growing, wheat policies and so on; and the more he talks the more I am convinced that the shepherd should stay with his flock.
The shepherd is trying to keep the wolves away from the flock.

And you are
doing a pretty good job. I have heard hon. members of this chamber, the leader of the opposition and others, speak of the effect of this policy on the live stock industry of eastern Canada. They claim that by what they call bonusing, though I do not call it that, in connection with coarse grains in western Canada, the farmers of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta will go more largely into the feeding of live stock and the raising of hogs, and that for this purpose they will take advantage of the so-called bonus to grow more coarse grains. After hearing these statements made yesterday I took the trouble to obtain the figures from the bureau of statistics. I find that last year there was a decrease of some 360,000 acres, as compared with the year before, in an acreage sown to oats in western Canada, while the acreage devoted to barley remained at practically the 1939 level. During the same period, however, the production of hogs in western Canada increased tremendously. Two points of view have been expressed in opposition to the vote proposed, one of them coming largely from western members-more by way of suggestion than of direct opposition 

and the other coming from members from the eastern part of Canada. The discussion which has taken place is only further proof of the fact that it is most difficult, in a country so far-flung as ours, to legislate with regard to an industry which is to be found in every

Supply-Agriculture-Wheat Acreages
province and have that legislation entirely satisfactory to every province. It is almost impossible to deal with any phase of agriculture in Canada by legislation or by a vote of this house and make it apply to all the provinces and have them all satisfied.
May I interrupt to say that that shows how difficult it is to govern Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Yes; it is one indication that Canada is difficult to govern. It is the reason, I think, why the only system under which Canada could remain a united country or under which the United States of America have been able to remain a united country is a federated system, that makes it possible in connection with certain matters to take slightly different action in one part of the country from what is done in another. For that reason quite a number of the problems which have been referred to during this discussion properly should be dealt with, in part at least, by the provincial governments. They have been giving assistance in certain directions in connection with agriculture; and what we do here alone1 cannot settle the problems which confront the people of Canada in relation to these different matters. It is difficult to do even those things we feel compelled to do, in a national way, in a manner that will give help to people in one section of the country without injuring those in other sections.
The western point of view, in so far as it has been critical, has been that this provision does not give the farmer of the west the same return he obtained last year, or even the year before, as a result of being able to sell his product, particularly wheat, even at the comparatively low advance the government found it possible to make. For example, the figures I have here indicate that in 1939 the return to the farmers of the three provinces particularly concerned with this legislation was approximately $336,000,000, while last year it was about $326,000,000, and over the last fifteen years it has been about $325,000,000 on the average. During quite a number of those years we were far below a return which made it possible for people to maintain themselves without receiving a great deal of relief.
Therefore, looking at the picture from that point of view, I do not think we are asking the committee or the people of Canada to do anjdhing unreasonable under this policy which, so far as it has been enunciated up to the present, makes possible a return to the western farmers of only $300,000,000. It is our hope that by having the policy varied in one way or another in the matter of administration, in connection with either the part under my
department or the part under the Department of Trade and Commerce, we may be able to bring that figure up to $325,000,000. At present, however, the figure is only $300,000,000, unless provision is made for an increase of $15,000,000 in farm produce other than wheat, which would be equal to the increase between 1939 and 1940 in connection with such produce. In other words, if this year there happens to be as great an increase in the returns from products other than wheat as there was last year, the total amount made available under the policy as it exists at present will be $315,000,000, leaving still another $10,000,000 to be found somewhere in order to bring the total return up to the average during the last fifteen years. That does not make any allowance for the fact that the cost of living is higher in western Canada, as in all Canada, than it was during the period of time for which that average is taken. Therefore I think it can be agreed that the amount of money which will be made available is not more than the house would be prepared to vote, by one method or another, in order to take care of that section of agriculture which has been injured by the position of the wheat market.
The objection from eastern Canada, as it has been expressed in this house up to the present, I think is to the effect that the greater production of coarse grains under the proposed policy will interfere with the sale of live stock and live stock products in eastern Canada; or, in other words, that, as a result of this policy, western farmers will come into competition with eastern farmers. A few moments ago the hon. member for Moose Jaw dealt with that situation and brought out the point that there had been a marked increase in the production of live stock and live stock products in western Canada before this policy was even discussed.
In that connection I have some figures which I think I should mention, particularly for the consideration of my hon. friends from Ontario. The number of hogs marketed in Saskatchewan in 1936 was 570,000; in 1940 it was 648,000. That represents an increase of only 13-7 per cent over our previous high year; and the only reason why the figures were lower in the interval was that one year we did not grow any grain, and we had to dispose of practically all our live stock. As a matter of fact, the Department of Agriculture went into Saskatchewan, bought the live stock, shipped it out and sold it. In the natural course of events that branch of agriculture had to come back; and if the number of hogs marketed last year was increased, that was not because of any policy put in force by this or any other government; it was because we grew grain in 1938

The point as to whether you feed hogs coarse grain or wheat does not enter into the question. The grain is there; wheat is there; rye is there. There is a shortage of barley and of oats, but the hogs can be fed wheat and rye, as far as the market is concerned, just as effectively as they can be fed coarse grains, although whether or not the bacon is quite as good I would not care to say. In other words, the fact that the production of coarse grains in western Canada will be increased will not bring about an increase in the number of hogs, any more than the fact that wheat is being stored in the west to-day would increase that number.
There is, however, one point that has been entirely left out of consideration. The leader of the opposition made reference to the fact that the governments of the eastern provinces had asked the federal government to ship or assist in shipping grain from west to east. The request that was made was not for the shipment of coarse grains, but for the shipment of wheat. The double argument was used that the wheat would be useful in producing live stock in the east, and relieve the storage of wheat in western Canada. The proposal made by those governments was that the federal government should deliver that wheat at a cost of fifty cents a bushel, paying half the
fMr. Gardiner.]
freight, in addition to delivering it at fifty cents a bushel from Fort William into eastern Canada. That meant that the dominion government was asked to take twenty cents a bushel or, if you like, to bonus the shipment of wheat to eastern Canada at twenty cents a bushel.

Did it
mean that?-because that is the No. 1 price.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: That is what it averaged up to. I have all the figures, but at this time I do not wish to take the time to put them on record. That, however, was the request.
I do not think that is quite correct.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
We substituted the suggestion that we were prepared to pay half the freight, provided the provincial governments would do likewise, on feed grains, whether it was on feed wheat or other grains.
As a matter of fact, in answer to what was said, there is very little feed wheat. That is the real reason why we could not have got
10,000,000 bushels. There is very little feed wheat to be found in the elevators at Fort William. That is the reason why it would be approximately twenty cents a bushel, when you figure it out on an average.

Supply-Agriculture-Wheat Acreages
But the coarse grains are there, and it was thought that with feed wheat, barley, rye and oats, there could be secured approximately
6.000.	000 bushels, and that by adding in some high-grade wheat it could be brought up to
8.000.	000 bushels, and be shipped to Ontario, the two governments paying half the freight. Only one province has taken that up.
Which one?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Ontario. We are paying to Ontario now half the freight on the feed grain which is being shipped from Fort William to feed the live stock in Ontario. That amounts to almost exactly the same per bushel as we are proposing to pay on the amount of coarse grain which is taken out of wheat-presuming that a farmer grows fifty bushels to the acre-and sown into coarse grains.
A point I would suggest to hon. members is that this policy will not, so far as we can see at the present time, influence one way or the other the production of live stock in western Canada. The thing that surprises me is that members from eastern Canada have not opposed the grass more strenuously than the grain. In western Canada we do not produce milk to any extent from feeding grain. It is too cold at the time we feed grain. In western Canada we produce milk from feeding grass. One has to have a fairly complete knowledge of farming conditions right across Canada in order to be concerned about some of the things which may happen as a result of putting into effect a certain policy.
I would therefore suggest to hon. members that from the beginning of the war we have been approaching this question from this point of view: We have been watching the development in connection with different branches of agriculture and in different sections of Canada. Up to date I think it will be agreed that when a real problem confronted the apple people, we dealt with it. An hon. member has said that a real problem confronts the potato growers, and that we have not dealt with it. One of the reasons why we have not dealt with it is that it has not been demonstrated to us that the war has made any difference in connection with the potato marketing problem. If it can be demonstrated to us that it has made a difference, I am sure the government will meet that problem in just the same manner as it has dealt with the problem connected with the apple crop.
Only the other day we had a delegation from the bean people. They were able to show that about one-third of their production had been marketed in Great Britain, and that to-day they are not able to market that
one-third. All we ask in cases of that kind is that the individuals or areas concerned, large or small, will take the problem first-if it is all within one province-to the provincial government concerned, and lay the problem before that government, suggesting the methods by which they w'ould like to have the matter considered. In that way the provincial government would take the responsibility for passing on to this government suggestions as to what ought to be done. I do not believe this government ought to go into Ontario and develop the production of beans by increasing the prices. We should not do that, thereby leaving a problem on the doorstep of the Ontario government.
But I do say this, that if by carrying out this policy the fears of eastern members are realized, in that we have produced too much coarse grain in western Canada, we should see to it that at least an equal advantage is given to the eastern farmer to get the use of that coarse grain-just as we have been doing this fall. If we give him an equal advantage to get the use of it, and if, as it has been said, by bonusing the farmer at so much an acre to produce so many bushels of coarse grains per acre we have made that grain available, then the grain ought to be made available to eastern farmers at a price correspondingly favourable to that at which it is made available to western fanners. We agree to that.
All I ask hon. members to do is to take for granted that what we have done in other cases will be done in this instance. When the problem arises, it will be dealt with on its merits, and it will be dealt with in a manner which will be satisfactory to the farmers in the different sections of Canada.
Mr. MacKENZIE CLambton-Kent): If I understand the minister correctly, this arrangement of paying half the freight is only a temporary arrangement to take care of scarcity due to adverse conditions-conditions which, under normal circumstances, would not occur in Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
No; there is not a shortage of grain in Ontario, as compared with some other years. In Ontario there is grain which has developed growths half an inch long because it was wet last fall, and could not be shipped out of the area. Shipments being made at the present time indicate that there is no great shortage of grain in Ontario. The fact that no grain has gone down into other sections is also an indication that there is no great shortage of it.
But the fact of the matter is this, that, as indicated by the figures put on record, there has been a great increase in the amount of live

stock not only in eastern Canada but in western Canada. The feeding of that live stock requires more coarse grains. If it is going to be properly fed next year, many farmers in Ontario will have to buy coarse grains, if they are going to increase their live stock production to the extent to which they indicate they are going to increase it. If we are going to be able to purchase coarse grains at prices which make possible the production of cheese, hogs, and so on, at a price which Great Britain and Canada combined can afford to pay for them -because the two governments will have to combine their financial ability to pay-we shall have to see to it that the feed is placed at the disposal of those who wish to consume it. For that reason we ought to assure ourselves that the feed is available. When we assure ourselves of that, let us see to it that the people who have live stock to feed, and have not the feed to feed them, get it at the lowest possible cost. This is what the policy has made possible.

speechtext: May I add just a word in regard to motions of this kind? While the government should be expected to give information on matters which are not readily ascertainable from public records and public documents, it is hardly reasonable to expect that the government should provide the means of collecting information for private members out of available documents. I hope that hon. members will not feel that their full rights and privileges are being in any way infringed if, where a return is requested for information which is already in public documents, the government refers hon. members to the documents themselves.

Prime Minister not carrying that principle just a little too far? Private members come into the house for the first time, say, after an election and they do not know where to turn for these things.
