speechtext:
I should like to ask a couple of questions of the Minister of Agriculture, and I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that they are entirely nonprovocative in character-in fact will have a rather soothing effect.

A statement has appeared in the Vancouver press within the last few days that reduced freight rates have been arranged for on the higher grades of wheat from the prairies to the coast, but it was somewhat indefinitely worded. As it is a matter of very considerable importance to British Columbia, could the minister state whether this has been arranged, and if so what the new rate is, and if, as asserted in the press, it is conditional on the wheat being mixed with coarse grains, how is the purchaser to be protected? Suppose for example a farmer or dealer buys a carload of grain guaranteed to contain only twenty-five per cent coarse grains, how is he protected against having sent him a carload containing forty per cent coarse grains?
While I am on my feet I would ask whether the word "wheat" in this connection will include, as it did in the original rate on which this is apparently based, the by-products of bran and shorts? Because dairy men and farmers do not want to feed their cows a mixture of wheat, barley and oats either ground or raw, and I do not think this reduction will be of much use to the dairymen unless they can get it on bran and shorts. It will benefit the poultrymen, of course.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: REDUCTION OF FREIGHT RATES WESTWARD ON MIXED GRAIN FOR FEEDING PURPOSES
speechtext:
The hon. member was kind enough to give me a copy of his question, and I give the following answer:
Representations were made to the department that the farmers in British Columbia were finding difficulty in obtaining sufficient quantities of the lower grades of wheat to meet their needs. Under CFA tariff 145 CTC 154, grains for feeding purposes may be carried at freight rates more or less intermediate between the regular export and domestic rates on grain from the prairies to British Columbia. This rate does not include wheat of grades higher than No. 4.
Representations were made to the railways to carry, during the present emergency, the higher grades of wheat for feeding purposes at the feed grain rates. They finally agreed to carry the higher grades provided they were mixed with other grain to make it difficult to use the grain for other than feeding purposes. In addition each shipment is accompanied by a certificate from the deputy minister of agriculture for British Columbia that, the grain is to be used for feeding purposes. In other words the railways will not accept the grain at the lower rates without the certificate from the deputy minister, who is supposed to satisfy himself that it will be used for feeding purposes. Under this arrangement it now will be possible for feeders in British Columbia to obtain any grade of wheat desired on the prairies, have it mixed with cereal

Wheat*-Coarse Grains
grains other than wheat before shipment, so that the resulting mixture when inspected will be graded by the inspector of the board of grain commissioners as mixed grain, and have it accepted and shipped by the railways at the feed grain rate.
The last question was whether bran and shorts could be included. Obviously it would be impossible to have bran and shorts included in these mixed grains; therefore it probably would be rather difficult to have bran and shorts come under these rates. But I would point out that all the ingredients of bran and shorts will be contained in the ground wheat, so that there should not be any serious difficulty about the matter so far as the general feeding of live stock is concerned. Of course where a farmer requires bran and shorts separate from the other grain, I understand that the regulation would not apply.

subtopic: REDUCTION OF FREIGHT RATES WESTWARD ON MIXED GRAIN FOR FEEDING PURPOSES
speechtext: The point is, of course, that bran is cheaper than wheat, and the dairyman does not want to buy an expensive feed like No. 4 wheat, when bran is a better milk producer.

At the time of the conference held to consider the report of the commission on dominion-provincial relations it appeared that the amount required for the whole year would be $850,000,000. That was the figure I gave to the conference. Had that turned out to be correct, this measure would ask for $150,000,000, not $135,000,000.
After parliament met the estimates were revised, and it appeared that the whole amount required for the year would be $875,000,000. Had that been correct I would be asking to-day for $175,000,000. As we have drawn nearer to the end of the fiscal year our estimates have of course become more accurate, and it now appears that the actual amount required will be about $135,000,000. That includes the provision of $15,820,700 for unforeseen contingencies. I cannot give the committee at this time particulars of the amount for contingencies, but the figures would show that that amount has been carefully worked out.

speechtext:
What is the present situation respecting restrictions placed on the travel of Canadians to the United States? The tourist season is opening shortly and I believe that in some of our cities fairly close to the boundary there is a feeling that the restrictions placed upon Canadians entering the United States are creating in the minds of the people of that country the impression that border crossing is extremely difficult. The result has been a great falling off in the influx of United States tourists into Canada. As the Minister of Finance knows, we have counted heavily upon the United States tourist trade for our

United States exchange. I suggest that perhaps the time has come when the restrictions upon Canadians entering the United States should be modified to some extent. The residents of the United States can travel only in the western hemisphere and we should make every effort to attract them to Canada. I am afraid that our tourist trade will be severely hit this season. Could the minister explain the situation at this time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR APPROPRIATION

Without having the regulations before me I can do so only in the most general terms. After giving the matter some

subtopic: WAR APPROPRIATION

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

subsubtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Our pleasure travel restrictions, if my memory serves me correctly, came into effect on July 1. The main reason for the falling off of tourist traffic from the United States to Canada was the passport regulations put into effect by that country.

subtopic: WAR APPROPRIATION
subsubtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is quite unexplainable because that is the reverse position. I should like to know upon what the minister bases his argument. He is making an assertion, but of course that is not proof.

subsubtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

The passport regulations were not understood and the people simply stayed home; for some reason or other they did not dare to come to Canada, It took the dissemination of considerable information to disabuse the minds of United States residents of that apprehension. In September and October there was a considerable increase in tourist business as compared with the previous months and the business came back practically to normal. It was comparable with the previous year.

subtopic: WAR APPROPRIATION

To what extent did our

subsubtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is the very point, and I see I shall have to go over this quite patiently. I have not the figures before me, but what I was pointing out is that the drop in tourist traffic occurred before the pleasure travel regulations came into effect. Later in the year there was a trend the other way. It is impossible to trace the cause and effect as between the pleasure travel regulations and the tourist business, but it is possible to see the cause and effect as between the passport regulations and the tourist business. Apparently the feeling held by some people is that if we were to abolish these regulations-

subtopic: WAR APPROPRIATION

speechtext: I did not say that.

subtopic: WAR APPROPRIATION

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR APPROPRIATION
subsubtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Let me finish the sentence- if we were to do away with the pleasure travel restrictions and allow this $60,000,000 or $75,000,000 to go to the United States, we would get that much or more than that through increased tourist travel to Canada. That might be so if there was a large disproportion between the amount which United States tourists spend in Canada and that which Canadian tourists spend in the United States. Canadians generally are under the impression that there is a great disproportion in these amounts. One very eminent gentleman who was concerned about this matter came to see me and told me he understood that the United States tourist spends about ten times as much in Canada as the Canadian spends in the United States when
1990	COMMONS
Supplementary War Appropriation Bill
travelling for pleasure. I told him that I thought the figure was more like three to one, and when I got the exact figure I found it was nearer to two to one. The proportion of our travel to theirs is surprisingly large. It is quite improbable that if we were to take down the bars and allow our people to visit the Florida beaches and the New York night clubs and other places where some Canadians in the past have liked to go, and let this $60,000,000 or $75,000,000 go to the United States, there would be a similar increase in United States tourist expenditure in Canada.
I do not like to be talking about the matter in this way. I do not know that one can sit down and put it on a purely dollar basis. I do not like to say that we should not spend a dollar unless we are sure we will get a dollar back. I should like to see no restrictions whatever upon travel between the United States and this country; I should like to see no passport regulations and no pleasure travel regulations or anything of the kind. But it must be remembered that we are buying such huge quantities of goods from the United States that there are some things which we must cease buying from that country. We cannot buy everything. We cannot buy all kinds of articles which were shut out under the War Exchange Conservation Act, allow our people to go on pleasure travel to the United States in a free and unrestricted manner, and at the same time pay hundreds of millions of dollars for munitions. The people of the United States understand that pretty well. If we were trying to keep our money here and get theirs, it would be a different thing, but as they well understand, we are not trying to do that. We are buying and buying and buying from the United States of America, and we are earnestly seeking ways in which we can keep ourselves in a position to continue to buy.
I do not believe it would be acceptable to the people of Canada if we were to ask those in the low income classes to deny themselves and to sacrifice, as we are asking them to do, making it impossible for them to import certain things which many of them regard as important, injuring seriously some importing businesses, as we have done by our War Exchange Conservation Act, and at the same time say to our people, "Go freely to the United States." It would look unfair on the face of it; it would be pretty hard to face down or to argue for. The only argument we could advance for such a proceeding would be that it would be good business for us to do that. But when, as I have said, normally the number of Canadian dollars spent in the United States is something like half the number of American dollars

spent in Canada, it is very improbable, if we were again to take down those bars and let our people go freely on pleasure travel in the United States, thereby depleting our stocks of exchange to the extent of sixty to seventy-five million dollars a year-which is a lot of money-that we would gain anything like that much from United States tourists who would come to Canada. All over the United States people are, progressively, realizing our situation. They understand that this country is at war, that it is putting forth a tremendous effort, and must conserve every dollar of United States exchange, not to keep it away from the Americans, but to spend it with them for things which will advance the prosecution of the war.
That is my conviction regarding this pleasure travel relaxation issue. I know that certain newspapers and individuals sincerely believe the contrary. They hold that we should try the effects of relaxation, but the risk is far too great for a government which has as one of its primary responsibilities the safeguarding of adequate stores of foreign exchange for a considerable period into the future.

subtopic: WAR APPROPRIATION
subsubtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
My suggestion was, not
that the restrictions should be abolished, but that the government should review them to see whether they might be relaxed to a certain extent. For example, it is almost impossible for Canadians to visit relatives in the United States. There are other factors to be considered. Railway companies, hotels, tourist agencies and bus companies have arrangements whereby they route tourists from one place to the other, and I doubt very much whether we can expect United States companies to route their citizens through Canada when there are no Canadians going down there. I should like to see something done in this direction. I hope for the sake of Canada that the government's policy is the correct one, but I suggest that further consideration be given to the advisability of relaxing these restrictions to some extent in the hope that a larger tourist trade from the United States will follow. They are only too anxious to help us in every way, but it is asking a lot for them to come up here when Canadians are unable to cross the border to see their friends. I doubt whether it is wise so to restrict the intercourse between the two countries.

subtopic: WAR APPROPRIATION
subsubtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Can the minister say whether as a result of the passing of the lease-lend bill it is intended to borrow from the United States?

subtopic: WAR APPROPRIATION

speechtext:
I cannot say. I do not know whether Canada will take advantage of the provisions of the lease-lend bill.

Supplementary War Appropriation Bill

subtopic: WAR APPROPRIATION
subsubtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I should
like to intervene briefly in this discussion on tourist traffic. The minister says the proportion is about two to one. That is far different from what we have been told over a period of years, when tourist agencies and boards of trade and similar bodies were agitating for increased grants from parliament and the provinces. It corresponds much more nearly to what my own view has always been, namely that so far as Canada is concerned this is a very ephemeral business-due in a large measure of course, to the shortness of our season, as well as to our failure adequately to advertise the attractions we have in this country for foreign visitors. I am astonished that the minister contends that it is only two to one.

subtopic: WAR APPROPRIATION
subsubtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: There is a lack of roads.

subtopic: WAR APPROPRIATION
subsubtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I think
the road situation has been taken care of reasonably well, having regard to our ability to foot the bill. In New Brunswick we have spent forty to fifty million dollars, which we could very ill afford, on the construction of roads to attract tourists. In the result we have not got back from the increased tourist traffic enough to take care of the carrying charges; we have had to resort to new taxation to build those highways. However, that was not the purpose for which I rose.
I think there is a lot in what the minister says. The imposition of the passport requirements on travellers going into the United States and the beginning of the falling off of the tourist trade into Canada more or less synchronized in point of time. I should not like to think that they represented cause and effect, although one might be driven to that conclusion. What I wanted to suggest to the government-now that such friendly relations have been established between the two countries, now that we are out to do all that we can for them, now that we are even going to let them build the waterway for us at their expense-was to ask the United States to withdraw the passport restriction upon the entry of Canadian nationals bona fide guaranteed and accounted for. That would do away with a lot of restrictions. If I want to go home by car to-day, it is almost an impossibility, even though I had the United States funds with which to pay my way through the United States; there is so much red tape about getting through. Now arrangements have been made for travel by rail. I come and go by train freely through Maine, to and from New Brunswick, but if I want to go to New Brunswick by automobile I have a lot of difficulty. The result is that both of us-they and I-lose something
which might be avoided if the passport restriction conditions were, at least, ameliorated. A much more friendly intercourse back and forth would be the result.
It occurs to me that the government could explore a number of other avenues for the saving of exchange. I am going to mention a case which came to my attention the other day. One of the contractors on an airport in the maritime provinces had as part of his contract-and an additional contract-a tremendous amount of trenching to do, and he got a good price for it. The prices for building these airports are good; I do not say they are too high or anything of the sort. The work had to be done in a hurry; we are told that speed is the first requisite. I realize that there is a great deal of truth in that. This contractor sublet the trenching to a man who did that class of work. It was profitable to the subcontractor, so much so that when the additional contract meant some miles of additional trenching the contractor would not give the man the new subcontract but sent $10,000 across to the United States to buy a new 10B Bucyrus-Erie trenching machine. He bought that machine to do the work himself.
This matter was brought to my attention by the subcontractor, who was out of a job and whose machine was idle. I brought it first to the attention of the foreign exchange control board and they said they had no jurisdiction; they were not policing importations. Then I brought it to the attention of the Minister of National Defence and he would have nothing to do with it; he said, "I have no authority". I will tell the minister that there is a tremendous amount of importations from the United States just in that category which should never be allowed, and one of the worst offenders is the building of the Canadian National railway terminal in Montreal. How much steel was imported into Canada during the last fiscal year to build the terminal of the Canadian National railway in the city of Montreal, using up important foreign exchange? The government is not a bit consistent. It will put the clamps on in one place but leave it wide open in another place.

subtopic: WAR APPROPRIATION
subsubtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Fruits and vegetables.

subtopic: WAR APPROPRIATION
subsubtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The other day a return was brought down showing importations of $22,000,000 worth of fruit and vegetables, which, with express and freight charges, would bring the bill up to $42,000,000 a year. It seems to me that the proper thing for the government to do is to review the whole position. Take my contractor friend: he should never have been allowed to import
1992	COMMONS
Supplementary War Appropriation Bill
that new machine, which was not made in Canada. The machine paid for itself in the one job-to him-but we lost $10,000 worth of exchange. I can give the minister the name of the contractor, the name of the subcontractor and the name of the machine he bought. These things have to be tightened up. I am not saying this in a complaining spirit. I am trying to help the minister on the question of foreign exchange, because I realize that while the situation with respect to United States exchange is not desperate-the minister did retract that word-it is very serious, and just what is the best way to meet it I do not know. I am not an expert and I would not undertake to advise the minister, but every day, every week and month sees a situation cropping up which, if it could have been foreseen-and it should be foreseen- would have materially altered the position.
I hope the minister will review the whole thing. American tourist traffic is important. If you can get that passport requirement lifted by the United States government it will go a long way to help the position. The difficulty is that a large number of tourists from the United States are former Canadians who are afraid to come over for fear that they will not be able to get back, although they may have been over there for thirty years. I know of a young lady who wanted to visit her sister. She came to Calais, Maine, and they sat and talked together on the doorstep of the customs house. She was afraid to come across for fear of the restrictions; she was afraid she could not get back. That is not a good position between the two countries to-day. We have a great ally in this matter in the person of our distinguished visitor here of a week or two ago, Senator Pepper of Florida. I am sure he will do everything he can to help the position. He knows the value of the Canadian tourist in his own state of Florida and he will help the government if they go after the thing man-fashion. Let us see if we cannot get some of these restrictions lifted.

subtopic: WAR APPROPRIATION
subsubtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
With regard to the
difficulties arising at border points, I concur entirely in what the leader of the opposition has said with reference to people who have been residents of the United States for fifteen or twenty years or more. They are afraid to come over here on account of the restrictions. Canadians may go over and take $5 in Canadian money to be used for emergencies and transportation, but this privilege serves only a limited purpose. I would urge the minister to give some further latitude. There are thousands of people in Canada and in nearby places in the United States, 
and even in places further inland across the border, who by reason of intermarriage desire to visit back and forth. Canadian visitors by signing a card can take $5 in Canadian money for emergencies and transportation only, but this is not satisfactory. While I was home in St. Catharines this week-end I learned of a number of people who wanted to go over for urgent reasons-illness among relatives, for example. I believe a definite extension of the privileges granted would greatly facilitate intercourse between Canada and the United States.
There is another matter I wish to mention particularly. The summer season is approaching and there will be a considerable movement of people to the Canadian west, crossing at Windsor and Sarnia, where they have to go through United States territory in their motor cars, in order to get to Saskatchewan and other parts of western Canada. I urge upon the minister the importance of facilitating communication, making things a little bit freer and easier for these people.
There is one other important point I wish to bring to the attention of the minister; it came to my notice over the week-end. In Camp Borden there is one hut with forty-two men including three Canadians; the rest are all Americans. They jocularly refer to the three Canadians as foreigners. One man from Massachusetts, who rode with me on the way to Ottawa, said that his wife was having to pay 18 per cent exchange in Massachusetts in order to get his money changed into American dollars. If there is any large percentage of such men in the air force and the army, as has been suggested to me on many occasions, every possible precaution should be taken to protect the interests of these boys who are serving their country for $1.30 a day. I ask the minister to see whether something can be done in cooperation with the Minister of National Defence or whoever is the proper authority to ensure that the pay of these soldiers shall be transferred on the ten per cent basis established between the two countries. I can give the name of the man who told me about the eighteen per cent. He said they had pleaded with their commanding officer asking if something could not be done to make sure that their wives did not suffer this hardship. Thousands of Americans are serving in our Canadian army and air force, and they should be protected in connection with exchange.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR APPROPRIATION
subsubtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I will look into these various suggestions and see what can be done.
The leader of the opposition made one or two suggestions about imports which he regards

Supplementary War Appropriation Bill
as unnecessary. Possibly there are unnecessary imports. But the difficulties of administration are tremendous. If, for example, we add machinery to part II of the War Exchange Conservation Act so that it can be imported only under licence or permit, the staff of the Department of National Revenue would have even more grief than they have at present.

subtopic: WAR APPROPRIATION
subsubtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I think you will have to come to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR APPROPRIATION
subsubtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: At the present time they find it almost impossible to know when to issue permits and when not to issue them to persons wishing to import articles listed in part II of the War Exchange Conservation Act. I receive representations from indignant wouldu be importers, although it does not come under my department, -and I know that the Minister of National Revenue receives ten or perhaps one hundred for every one I receive. I assure the committee it is no easy matter to pick and choose as between importers and to say to A that he may import and to B that he may not.

subtopic: WAR APPROPRIATION
subsubtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: You have to know the facts in every case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR APPROPRIATION
subsubtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

What the minister is saying in relation to this position amounts to this, that our fiscal policy is being dictated by Washington. This government are so fearful of offending the United States that they will not protect our own nationals. There is the position in a nutshell. You sacrifice the market gardeners and fruit and vegetable growers of this country to appease the United States government, whose own nationals put pressure upon them. If that is not dictation I do not know what is. We had the same position in the last Dunning budget prior to the 1930 change. Hon. gentlemen opposite know what happened because of that very position, and it will happen again if the Canadian public begin to understand. We ought to assert our fiscal independence and point out to the United States government- surely they are amenable to reason-that never before in the history of this nation have we spent so much money with them. True, it is for goods of a different class or kind, but we are buying more from the United States than we ever did, and how we are going to pay for it in the days to come is a puzzle to me. The minister will find, and the United States government will find, before we are through that there will have to be further restrictions; unnecessary luxuries from the southern states, such as Florida strawberries, will have to be shut out. They do not amount to much after all.
There is a principle at stake as well as a question of expediency. Surely the United States authorities are not so obtuse, shall I say, as not to know that their trade with Canada has always been one of the bulwarks of their export trade. How this little country has paid the millions of dollars of adverse balances that have grown up in connection with our trade with the United States has been almost beyond me. We never would have been able to do it if we had not had the greatest customer in the world on the other side of the Atlantic, which enabled us to settle our accounts on a three-cornered basis. I heard my late chief, Mr. Bennett, make a speech on this subject. From 1867 to 1930 the adverse balances of trade against this country, as between imports and exports between Canada and the United States, came to an astonishing figure, not millions but billions. We paid that adverse balance by exporting to the mother country, though a good deal of it was paid by exporting our estate, our raw materials which should have been manufactured in this country.

That may be so, but as one of the hon. members who represent constituencies having certain specialized types of agriculture I feel that something further should be brought to the attention of the minister at this time with regard to the orchard men and the growers of vegetables. There is a little more to this whole problem than the minister has stated. It may be true that representations on behalf of our own growers have been given consideration, but there is another angle to this matter that I think should be kept in mind. There are other influences, in this country as well as in the United States, which somewhat conflict with the interests of the growers themselves. After the foreign exchange conservation act had been passed in this house I was amazed at some of the comments that were made in the United States with regard to this industry. I should be the first to admit that nothing should be said in this house that would reflect in any way upon the United States government or people. We are all in this thing together, and perhaps it is very largely a question of conflicting interests within both countries rather than of any conflict between the countries or the governments themselves.
In the New York Packer of December 7 last there appeared a very interesting and enlightening article-later reprinted by the Canadian food distribution council-which I think is rather important. Mr. William Garfitt, the executive vice-president of the United Fresh Fruit and Vegetable Association in the United States, was discussing the failure of the Canadian government to impose any embargo, as he termed it, upon the importation into this country of fresh fruits and vegetables under that act. As most hon. members will recall, there was a good deal of rumour and gossip to the effect that the importation of fresh fruits and vegetables was to be in some way restricted, and evidently 14873-1261
this article was written with that idea in mind, because it comments on the good fortune of the United States growers in not having to face this problem. Addressing himself to the growers of the United States, Mr. Garfitt had this to say:
Last week I was able to tell you that, partly through the efforts of your association, the Canadian government had decided to modify an almost total embargo on fresh fruit and vegetable imports from the United States, and to exclude only a limited number of perishable commodities. This week I am happy to be able to report that the embargo has been lifted entirely, and that any American fruit or vegetable can enter the dominion without restriction.
This will be good news, not only to American growers, but to wholesalers and commission merchants, who were confronted with what seemed the necessity of finding home markets for close to $20,000,000 worth of products. . . .
That is about the value of our yearly importations from the United States, without including freight and so on.
. . . that would otherwise have been exported to Canada. Other industries were not so fortunate, as entire classes of goods, such as automobiles, radios, canned fruits and wearing apparel, are on the list of prohibited "nonessentials".
This is something which concerns all of us. The minister will understand that I am not in any way critical of him, but I believe this should be placed on the record so that we may know what influences other people believe are brought to bear on the situation. He goes on to say:
Just what caused the Canadian Minister of Finance, Mr. J. L. Ilsley, to make such an abrupt aboutface will probably never be known. But I believe your association can take some credit for it. When the threat of embargo became known some two or three weeks ago, I conferred with the Canadian jobbers in Toronto-
In ordinary farm parlance, this looks like the nigger in the woodpile. In any event
he says:
-I conferred with the Canadian jobbers in Toronto, suggesting to them that they send a delegation to Ottawa to protest that fresh fruits and vegetables should be admitted as a public health measure.
He goes on to say:
Immediately following the Toronto conference, the United-
That is, United Fresh Fruit and Vegetable Association of the United States-
-started a stream of protest flowing through the United States Department of Agriculture, the Treasury department and the Department of State to the Canadian ministry of finance, pointing out that any such restriction on the movement of American agricultural goods would jeopardize the reciprocal trade treaties in effect between the United States and Canada. This seemed to have considerable bearing in the minister's decision.

This incident seems to be a good example of what an alert trade organization can do if given aggressive backing by its members and by others in the industry it serves.
In response to our telegrams to shippers and important handlers of fruits and vegetables in all parts of the country, the industry began at once to make its voice heard in official Washington-and official Washington had no choice but to lay the facts of the matter before the Canadian authorities.
Perhaps this is pertinent in view of the fact that the budget is coming down. The minister should be well advised so that he may say to this organization that he is independent of it. The article continues:
This does not mean however that all danger of future embargoes has been disposed of. In its anxiety to conserve every dollar of its liquid resources for war material purchases, the dominion is likely to revive this so-called economy measure. In that event, we shall be ready to go to bat again, but in the meantime it would seem to be only the part of wisdom for American shippers and receivers to do everything in their power to stimulate consumption in their home markets.
In other words, they are getting ready for changes which the minister may make in his budget.
It will be understood that I do not place this on record for the purpose of criticizing the minister. I realize the position in which he finds himself, and I would be the first to sympathize with him. It must be remembered that here in Canada two different and sometimes conflicting influences are being brought to bear, one by those whose business it is to make money from the importation of fresh fruits and vegetables, and the other by those who are connected with the growing of fresh fruits and vegetables for our own consumption.
The placing of this article on the record may serve to bring to the attention of the minister the type of influence being brought to bear in the trade in the United States.
The view seems to be held that the Canada-United States trade agreement might be jeopardized in some respects through the placing of restrictions on importations of fresh fruits and vegetables. I have not been greatly influenced by that bogy of altering trade agreements. It has always been said to the other farmers, "If you people want restrictions on fresh fruits and vegetables, then you must be prepared to lose some of your cattle quota or your cattle market in the United States." Of course that has had some effect on the public mind. No one wants our cattle market curtailed but I have never been convinced that that would be the result, because, as the minister very properly pointed out-and I was glad he did so-we are not attempting to curtail our purchases in the United States.
fMr. Ilsley.]
The fact is we are trying to expand them. In order to expand them we ask simply that we be given by means of these restrictions more money with which to make such expansion. In my opinion no interests in the United States can properly take exception to what I am saying, because, after all, the money is being used for one purpose only, that of keeping industry in the United States moving so that it may provide war materials for us.
I would ask the minister when preparing his budget again to give consideration to this matter of the importation of fresh fruits and vegetables. It is a serious matter, because it is double-barrelled so far as we are concerned. The growers are having a tough time of it-and when I use those words I believe I am speaking as fairly as possible. Their difficulties are increasing because of the increased costs of production. In addition they are experiencing labour scarcity, and to the gardeners particularly that is a great difficulty. On top of that, the influx of United States products has seriously decreased their market. I make a sincere and urgent plea to the minister to give further consideration to this one method of conserving foreign exchange.
I do not believe any of us would ask for a complete restriction or a complete embargo. I do not believe the fresh fruits and vegetable growers themselves would want any hon. member to make that suggestion. But there are certain restrictions which might properly be made. I ask the minister to give careful study to the whole question of the importation of fresh fruits and vegetables, basing his conclusions entirely, if he wishes, on the question of conservation of foreign exchange, and leaving out consideration of the growers. We have here a chance to save at least something of the $43,000,000 exchange position which we are trying in so many other ways to guard and protect. While our imports into Canada of fruits and vegetables are valued at something like $21,500,000, we must double that amount when we add freight and other charges which the Canadian consumer has to pay.
I make this earnest plea to the minister. Our great agricultural industry needs help. Here is a chance to help it, and at the same time to help our foreign exchange position. The Minister of Finance has an opportunity in this instance to do both, with the same stroke of the pen.

I am really going further than that, because I have gone into the matter in some detail. I think my hon. friend realizes, and I believe the committee will realize, that this is probably the most difficult task which could fall to one. I do not think I am unduly secretive, but at the same time there are in connection with equipment a great number of matters regarding which the staff are positive that information should not be given. I am between the upper and the nether millstones. On the one hand, the committee wants all the information possible, as do the public. On the other, the staff very
properly points out to me that I am the head of a department which has an intelligence service part of whose work is to see that subversive activities are not carried on, and part of these subversive activities is to endeavour to get information with regard to types and production of equipment being produced in this country. The staff at headquarters find it hard to see why the minister, simply because he desires to be as frank as possible, should be giving information which spies would give their lives to get and for which other countries would pay a great many hundreds of thousands, perhaps millions of dollars.
I am going to give the best information I can, and I am afraid I shall be erring on the side of giving more than I should. The tabling of the MacMillan report by my colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply was not regarded with equanimity by the staff at national defence headquarters. It was, however, deemed necessary to table that report in view of a situation which had arisen. That is water over the dam. I do not wish to go further in that direction by way of forecasts, predictions and the giving of figures. Let me say this further, because I think it is time that we had a frank discussion and a frank study of the situation. You do not find the Prime Minister of Great Britain making any statements with regard to the number of aeroplanes or the number of ships or the number of anything else. You do not find Mr. Eden or Mr. Margesson rising in his place in the British House of Commons and outlining the situation in connection with various items of equipment which are being produced for the army. You do not find Lord Beaverbrook giving the number of aeroplanes. Those gentlemen are said to have been extremely frank, and they have been frank in stating that there have been discouragements, delays and so on-these have occurred in Canada as well-but they have not given any figures.

I am going to begin with what is perhaps one of the most difficult items, at least so far as the army is concerned. I refer to the

matter of field guns, anti-tank guns and antiaircraft guns. The making of these guns is in the hands of four of the most reputable, efficient and best known Canadian firms. The fact is that so far the army has not received delivery of any of these guns. The committee will be glad to know that anti-aircraft gun barrels have, as has already been stated by my colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply, been delivered and been found to be eminently suitable for the purposes of substitution for barrels in guns which have been used already. I may say also that we expect very shortly to have some anti-tank guns for training purposes.
The situation with regard to 25-pounder guns has been particularly scrutinized by my colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply. I told the house some days ago that we had a definite understanding with our friends in Great Britain with regard to field guns. The committee will realize that 25-pounders are being produced in the same plant in Canada for both British and Canadian account. There is no lack of recognition of their importance by us or by the Department of Munitions and Supply. My colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply, and his staff know how much we should like to have these guns just as soon as possible. I feel that it is due to both the minister and his staff to say that they certainly have put their backs into trying to get these weapons for us.
There is nothing to be discouraged about. We have approximate target dates for the delivery of these weapons, and I am sure that Canadian industry will strain every nerve to see that we get them. While I am speaking of this matter of target dates, perhaps I may say something else-my colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply referred to this the other night-with reference to the matter of forecasts. My officers go to the Minister of Munitions and Supply from day to day to ask him when they may get this, that and the other article, and I think my colleague is getting just a little weary of that sort of thing. He tells them, "If I do tell you, you will hold me to it, and when the time comes, you will say that you are getting it two or three weeks late." Here is what he says now, "I will tell you that we will get them just as soon as Canadian industry can fill the order, and we have placed it in reliable hands."
I have to say to my colleague that this is really not good enough for me, although I appreciate his position. I should like to have some sort of target date so that I can make plans to equip certain formations with certain types of weapons. I tell him that if a target date is set, it will assist us in making our

plans ind will encourage industry to live up to that date. I think we should all realize that this is not a matter which concerns only the Department of Munitions and Supply. It is a matter particularly for Canadian industry. That department passes on to us what it gets from the particular industry which is engaged in making the particular piece of equipment. We ought to realize, and we in national defence have to realize, as does munitions and supply, that industry is engaged-I am speaking particularly of weapons-in the manufacture of something which has never been manufactured in Canada before. They are trying to do their very best with plans and specifications, drawings and tools, and dies and jigs, getting machine tools from everywhere, and adapting their plant facilities accordingly. Probably there is a tendency on the part of industry to make us a little happier by saying that they will make their deliveries at a certain date-finding afterwards that unexpected difficulties have arisen. At the same time I do not wish to discourage industry or munitions and supply from giving us the best forecasts they can in order to help us make our plans. If they do their level best to live up to those forecasts, that is all we can ask of them.
In the meantime, we of the service departments to whom these particular weapons are coming are not going to lie down and say that because equipment does not come faster, we cannot do anything. We try to help by agreeing on a different priority, so that this particular thing may receive more attention and something else may get less, in order to obtain the particular weapon we desire. We endeavour also to do our best to use what we have, or get along with some sort of substitute, until we receive the particular weapon we want.
In connection with anti-tank weapons, we have been training right along with 18-pounders. They are not the ideal thing, but our artillerymen are used to them, and training for anti-tank work is extremely desirable and has had good results.
Speaking of anti-aircraft guns, we are using for training purposes such equipment as there is in this country. We are not groaning about the fact that we cannot get more anti-aircraft weapons immediately. They will come. We are sending personnel overseas in order that they may be familiar with this weapon when the units go over, and also to enable some of the men to return and give instruction on this side in the use of these weapons.
I emphasize this-and it goes back to the question which the hon. member for Yale was asking-that our Canadian production of these articles must be used to the very best

Supplementary War Appropriation Bill
advantage. A small number are utilized for training here, but the bulk of the production goes to the United Kingdom, because we believe that to be the sound distribution; after all, we expect them to be used by our men overseas.
With regard to anti-tank rifles, as the committee knows, engineering and production of these rifles were put in the hands of the Inglis company by the new contract which was made late last fall, and my assurance is that every effort is being made to manufacture them as quickly as possible.
As regards the 2-inch and 3-inc'h mortars, deliveries of 3-inch mortars have actually been made; and manufacture of 2-inch mortars is under way, but it will be a considerable time. I believe, before deliveries are received.
I am advised that we have sufficient Lee-Enfield rifles for operational purposes in Canada. For training requirements and for the reserve army we are depending mainly on the rifles which we got from the United States, plus sufficient Lee-Enfields for firing practice.
In November I said something to the committee about the steps which were being taken to increase our stock of rifles. My colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply has been successful in that respect, and there are now additional rifles on the way to add to our stocks from the United States. These, I am advised, will suffice for our requirements until Canadian production begins. I can assure him that that is not the situation to-day. Bren guns are now being issued on what we consider to be an adequate training scale to the formations of the active army and also the training centres in this country. What is, perhaps, more important to the committee, all active units proceeding overseas will be equipped to full establishment, I believe, with Bren guns before they leave.
My hon. friend asked about Bren guns for training centres. I expect that at the present rate of production and on the present scale of distribution, all training centres will be adequately equipped by the end of May.
My hon. friend asked for information regarding the rate of output for Bren guns. As I have intimated, I am not going to give the figures, but I can come very close, because of the fact that the figures are mentioned in the contract. I can say, what I am sure will
be satisfactory to him and the committee, that, as this month ends, there will have been delivered three times the number of completed guns which the contract called for up to this date. Further than that, in order to help in the front line until our additional formations get there, Canada is shipping directly overseas about one-third of the guns she is getting. That is, of course, in addition to the British allotment under the contract, which is also going overseas.

The committee will remember that I indicated that the establishment of machine gun units had been substantially lowered, and therefore as many guns were not required. We consider that we have sufficient for our coast defence units and for the advanced training centres. I believe that I mentioned last November that we had machine gun units which were surplus to this new establishment; that is to say, the new establishment which had come into force required less machine gun units, and therefore we had some surplus. Since that time we have converted two of them into other types of units. There may be further changes along that line.
There are some reserve machine gun units; whether they will be retained as such is a problem. If they are, we could do with more machine guns; but as matters stand, we consider that we have sufficient on hand to enable training to be carried on effectively for such units as are required.
Regarding field guns, I spoke a moment ago of the 25-pounders, and I wish to repeat what I said in November, that we have sufficient at least to equip the third and fourth divisions. Our plans are that only a portion of the field guns of the third division will be sent to England, and the remainder of this equipment will be supplied from United Kingdom sources. The committee will remember that our supply of field guns was augmented last summer. I will not mention the number, but it was substantial. Practically all of those, that is about six-sevenths of them, have already been high-speeded, as have all the 18-pounders. The field guns which we have

are, in the opinion of our staff, quite sufficient for training and for Canadian defence until 25-pounders are available. I do not think there is anything more I can say about the 25-pounders. As I stated last November, the Minister of Munitions and Supply has indicated and still indicates that a substantial number will be forthcoming this year. I had a full discussion about them with the war office. I have just mentioned our understanding with regard to the scale of equipment of field guns for the third division.
In the earlier stages of the production of 25-pounders it is likely that the bulk will be sent overseas to equip empire forces including our own. I should think that probably we would retain in this country only the minimum until production gets into its stride-that is, the minimum essential for training purposes. As a matter of fact, we have that arrangement now with the British.
With regard to universal carriers, this weapon is new to the war, but at the same time it is a most interesting one. Here again I am not going to give the committee the numbers of deliveries. Deliveries have commenced at a good rate, and our purpose is to make the best use of these carriers as they come off the line. What we are doing, to take full advantage of them, is to divide them up between Canada and overseas. For Canadian requirements, we have in mind training the units which are earmarked for formations planned for this year. To be more specific, I can say that at the present rate of production-even if there were no increase-our requirements on the training scale for the training centres in Canada and for active formations in this country will be filled, according to present calculations, in three months.
Let me say this in the same connection. We have made a schedule of deliveries for all the units and training centres which we think need these carriers, and we have allotted the exact number to be given to each, the order in which they are to be given, according to what our officers regard as priority. We have every unit's requirements planned out and have provided for the number which each unit should have in turn in the earlier stages. That includes not only units in Canada but those in the outposts as well, particularly in Newfoundland and Iceland. That is so far as Canada is concerned.
As I have said, we are making the allotment in two parts, part for Canada and part for Britain. The allotments for the United Kingdom will give us a large volume over there to complete the equipment of the corps, including the third division. To give the

committee a general idea, perhaps I shall be going further than I ought to. I can say, however, that at the present rate of production, without any increase-and my colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply will say that we are really just getting into our stride now-we shall have received in six months enough carriers to provide the initial war establishment equipment for every unit and formation of the Canadian army both overseas and here-that is, the Canadian active army. That is not taking into consideration the carriers which have already been issued to the units of the corps overseas through British sources.
Regarding signal equipment, my hon. friend the member for Yale discussed this question, mentioning the difficulty with the technical units and the trouble they are having in training without sufficient up-to-date equipment. These difficulties have been realized from the beginning. As I have explained on more than one occasion, we were advised, and we felt that there seemed to be no alternative, to get the British pattern equipment so as to have it interchangeable, and we put two of the outstanding firms in electrical apparatus to work on that job. I had a talk with the manager of one of them only last Saturday. There had been a setback in the target date he had given originally. That setback is over now because deliveries are being made in this particular type of equipment. I said to him, "How is it that you have had to set your date back?" He replied, "I must confess that there were 2,000 items, different bits and pieces in that particular piece of mechanism. We had to plan for tools, dies and jigs to deal with each one of these parts, and to be quite frank, we underestimated by a considerable percentage the number of machine tools that would be required." That is understandable, when they are working under pressure One cannot find fault. I am glad, however, that we had a target date to shoot at, even if there were delay, because I am sure it helped to some extent in making the delivery as prompt as it has been.
There have been disappointments and delays in the production of wireless sets-I believe wireless sets are what my hon. friend referred to particularly-but I am pleased to say that deliveries of sets of one pattern will begin, not in a few months or in a few weeks, but in a very few days, and the rate of delivery is expected to be such that our requirements will be complete within a month. The other wireless set will be rather slower, beginning in May, but this will not interfere with

training, although we want them as quickly as possible. In the meantime, we have had a certain amount of wireless equipment in the training centre, and such equipment has been augmented by commercial line telephone sets adapted to army use. We have received these in large numbers. We are now also receiving satisfactory deliveries of standard field telephones in very large quantities.
With reference to signals lights and so on, I might mention that orders have been placed. Some deliveries have been coming in and we anticipate no delay.
My hon. friend mentioned motorcycles. I would remind him that the motorcycle unit as such is no more, so far as the Canadian active army is concerned. All of them have been converted into units of the Canadian armoured corps. Of course, some motorcycles are needed for units that are not actually motorcycle units, but we have been able to procure all motorcycles which we considered were required. My hon. friend may have had in mind some particular case in which they have been short, but we have been able to procure all the motorcycles which in our opinion were required for training up to the present, and we do not anticipate any difficulty in meeting the needs for the future for such motorcycles as may be required for army purposes. Motorcycles are not manufactured in Canada, or have not been up to date, and we have procured requirements from England and, later, from the United States. Probably the Minister of Munitions and Supply would tell the committee that for the future such requirements as we have will likely be filled from the United States, because the type we use in the army is practically standard production there.

With regard to mechanical transport I do not think the committee will expect me to take much time. We regard the situation as good. As the committee know, we have been supplying large quantities not only to the Canadian forces but to empire forces overseas, and I think Canadian transport played a substantial part in the Libyan campaign a few weeks ago. The only limitation placed on the issue of mechanical transport to troops in Canada has been due to the fact that one hundred per cent establishment is not needed for training. We could have supplied more if needed; there is in fact a surplus available above our present requirements. The committee will be particularly interested to know that the formations proceeding overseas, for instance, will be fully equipped from Canadian production. I should perhaps except a few-only a few-special type vehicles which are not manufactured in this country and which it would be economically unsound to procure here, a few of which are needed for each division. I think the committee listened to Mr. Wallace Campbell's statement when he spoke a few weeks ago with regard to the production of mechanical transport for army service purposes.
With regard to munitions, provision has been made for all small arms artillery ammunition required for operational purposes and training in this country. In addition, small arms ammunition is being produced in enormous quantities for British account. Our policy in connection with this production is to ship overseas everything we possibly can; what our forces require there will be met from that supply. On account of the urgency of the situation abroad, we deliberately planned to retain in this country only a sufficient amount for operational necessities and for the training of the troops here.
In connection with gas respirators, I spent an interesting Saturday afternoon at the gas respirator assembly plant here. I think hon. members would be interested in visiting it. Respirators are being assembled at our own plant at the research building; they are being delivered in large quantities and within a month or so, all the active formations will be fully equipped. Production is in excellent shape. Production has been such that if we had used them all for the Canadian fighting forces, we would have met the full requirements of the active army, the navy and the 
air force. Production, however, was diverted a bit to promote increased deliveries on a big order from south Africa. The army already has had enough to provide initial equipment for all the active army both here and overseas and for one-third of the reserve ranks as well. We anticipate that there will be no trouble in filling all requirements on time, as they are needed.
That is a brief resume of the equipment situation. I happen to be the customer; my colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply is to some extent the supplier-at least he is the procurer; the real supplier is Canadian industry. I have faith that Canadian industry will do the job that is before them. They have had disappointments and discouragements; those have been translated into some setbacks and discouragements to us. As I have indicated, however, we are not lying down; we are going ahead full blast endeavouring to make the best use of what we have, seeing that the cardinal policy is observed, that is, to send overseas all we possibly can, also doing everything we can to speed up production by regulating our priorities. We in the Department of National Defence will not rest until we have everything to equip our troops. We are not boasting but we do feel that substantial progress has been made and that the serious shortage of equipment which I mentioned both in July and November is being gradually but, I think, surely overcome.

speechtext:
The house resumed from Thursday, March 20, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Howe-Mr. Vien in the chair:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Trans-Canada Air Lines Act, 1937, changing the period for the fixation of rates for the current year, as defined in the act, and extending the initial period during which a subsidy may be payable to Trans-Canada Air Lines.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OP INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD- CHANGING OF FIXATION-OP-RATES PERIOD
speechtext: What is the background of the proposal?

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES EXTENSION OP INITIAL SUBSIDY PERIOD- CHANGING OF FIXATION-OP-RATES PERIOD
speechtext:
This proposal was discussed at great length about a week ago; and at that time, although we had to report progress in order to let another item of business go through, I believe the discussion had about ended. This is a proposal which changes the act to the extent that compensation for the carriage of mail is not fixed automatically but is fixed arbitrarily. Owing to the fact that the expansion of the line is quite rapid, the arbitrary figure set out in the act is, under present circumstances, hardly fair to the post office. In other words, this permits us to change the rate per mile for carrying mail from an automatic rate of 53 cents to a negotiated rate of 40 cents. Also it changes

National Parks-Prince Albert
the period in which the new rate shall apply so that it runs from the first of April to the first of April, instead of from the first of January to the first of January.

subtopic: PRINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, all of us realize the great benefits of parks in providing an opportunity for healthy relaxation and also for the conservation of game. This committee should have an explanation from the minister why the Prince Albert national park is to be reduced in area, as is set out in the bill. The reduction in area will be approximately one-fifth. This is the only national park in Saskatchewan. If my memory is correct, it was established in 1927, following the election of the Prime Minister in the constituency of Prince1 Albert.
The reasons given by the minister when the bill was introduced were, as I understood them: first, that the area which is being removed from the park boundaries is to be so removed because it is swampy. May I point out that, in so far as the eastern portion ol the park is concerned, that area is covered ir the main with timber, and that this timber is valuable and, I think, necessary to the preservation of the water courses within that park.
The main reason given for cutting down the area of this park is that it will reduce the cost of fire ranging; but when we look at the estimates for the year 1941-42, it is apparent that that cannot be the reason for reducing the area of the park. At page 116 of the estimates for 1941-42, under the heading of "temporary assistance," there is an amount of $95,789, a reduction of some $8,000 as compared with the preceding year; but under the head of "wages" there is an increase of $30,000 among the various parks throughout the dominion.
The stand of timber in the eastern portion of this park is a valuable one, and it is being sought by certain interests in northern Saskatchewan who are endeavouring, I understand, to obtain an opportunity to take over this area of timber. For that reason I protest against the reduction in the size of the
National Parks-Prince Albert

park. Lumber is needed now, yes; but there are other places in northern Saskatchewan where timber is available. As regards the argument that a part can be set aside for settlement, there is a great deal of land there for settlement without reducing the area of a park which up to the present time has been generally accepted as being of the proper size.
The minister has stated that there has been no request from the government of Saskatchewan to reduce the area of the park. The explanation is that there is a saving in the cost of fire ranging. That, however, is scarcely tenable having regard to the estimates that have already been given, and I should like the minister to give a further explanation, showing the committee in detail what that saving will be. I point out to him, as he already knows, that no other areas are available in the future that will allow for any addition to the park. I should like to have a full explanation from him.

subtopic: PRINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext:
There is little to add to
the explanation I gave when the bill was in the resolution stage. The hon. member for Lake Centre rather hints that there is something dark and mysterious behind the suggestion that the area of the park be reduced. There is nothing to that, further than the degree to which it exists in the hon. member's imagination. As a matter of fact, as I stated when the bill was in the resolution stage, the recommendation came to me from the officials of the department. It did not come from any member of the Saskatchewan government or from anyone who might be interested in timber. It is true that there is some timber in this area which is being taken out on the eastern boundary of the park. As I stated previously when the matter was before the committee, there are three separate blocks being removed from the park. One of them, the largest one, is the eastern portion of the park now and consists, as I stated before, of swampy land and timber. I never said that there was not a certain amount of timber being taken out of the park. I stated before that the area was timber and swampy land, and I stand by that. That is the area on the eastern boundary. The added economy may not be very great, but it will amount to something.

the expense of a couple of timber rangers. In addition to that, there is the maintenance of a portion of the road that runs through the park to Montreal lake which, when this area is removed, will become the burden of the Saskatchewan government.

subtopic: PRINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES

it anyway.

subtopic: PRINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext: At any rate, I can tell the hon. member that it will not be paid by the parks branch, and that is what I am mainly interested in. Then there is a small area of eleven square miles which is to be added to an Indian reserve. I was in error the other evening when the leader of the opposition asked me if that provision would be in the bill. The arangement is that these areas are transferred to the province, and by agreement with the province certain lands are transferred back to the federal government for Indian reserve purposes.

subtopic: PRINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext: Why is that method followed?

subtopic: PRINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext: It is the simplest method of dealing with the matter, and I always believe in pursuing simple rather than complex methods.

subtopic: PRINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext: It would not appear to me to be so. Title is now vested in the crown in the right of the dominion; all you have to do is by proper order in council, or. if necessary, by this bill, to transfer it to the Indian Affairs branch, and the title never changes.

subtopic: PRINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext: Except for this-and I speak subject to correction-that in the transfer agreement under which the resources were returned to the province, any land set aside for park purposes that ceased to be used for this purpose would be returned to the province. This, at any rate, is the simplest method of dealing with the matter. The reduction is not nearly so serious as the hon. member for Lake Centre supposes. The area of the park at the present time is 1,870 square miles. What is taken out is 376 square miles, and of that a block of eleven square miles comes back to the government to increase the area of the Indian reserve, which we need rather badly.

subtopic: PRINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext: Is it the swamp that goes to the Indian reserve?

subtopic: PRINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES
speechtext: The timber in the muskeg area does not go to the Indians. The land that is being added to the Indian reserve is fair agricultural land. That is the description given me, and I have no reason to doubt it.

speechtext: How much timber is in the part that is going to the Saskatchewan government?

subtopic: PRINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES

National Parks-Prince Albert

subtopic: PRINCE ALBERT-PROVISION FOR WITHDRAWING CERTAIN AREAS OF LAND AND ESTABLISHING NEW BOUNDARIES

It was thought this land was not necessary for park purposes and it was believed we could save a few thousand dollars by allowing it to revert to the province.
Some hon. members have referred to the timber and have asked why we do not keep control of the timber and realize on it. That is not the purpose for which these parks were created. It is true that when trees become overripe in some of the parks, we sell some cordwood, but that is because the

National Parks

Prince Albert
land is required for park purposes. Here we do not require it for park purposes, and when the National Parks Act was passed, it was not the intention that the national parks would be developed for the purpose of obtaining a profit from the timber resources in the parks. It is being

Here we have an area with God-given facilities to retain moisture, including muskeg, rivers and lakes, which are all too few in that great province, and tall trees which, no doubt, timber exploiters are looking at with anxious acquisitiveness. Yet, on the one hand, the Minister of Natural Resources presumes to tell us that his department is going to save the expense of three or four timber cruisers in this area, for the benefit of the hard-pressed treasury of Canada, while on the other hand, the Minister of Agriculture says, "Hand it over to me, and I will give them S4 an acre to summer-fallow it or $2 an acre to grow grass on it". I agree with hon. members on this side that we have heard very little sound reason why this section of the park should be taken back. Even in Ontario, where perhaps we are more in need of land, it would be wise policy for any government to retain an. area such as that to conserve moisture through its trees, and its lakes and streams, which without doubt would dry up with such a development as the minister suggests. It seems to me a pennywise and pound-foolish policy to take part of that great province of Saskatchewan, which needs muskeg, which has not too many trees, or lakes, or streams, and hand back 240,000 acres which are ideally adapted to retain moisture. I suggest that the minister reconsider this recommendation of his parks branch, and I advise him to be very careful in approving any such recommendation from them.
I recall the time when this park was inaugurated, and I also remember some reasons for its inauguration. Back in 1926 the Prime Minister, who should be here to-night to tell us what he thinks about it, informed us that a great playground was to be established in the province; it was to have an area of 1,500 square miles. As one hon. member has mentioned to-night, if it is too large now it must certainly have been too large then. The Prime Minister, however, during his first election campaign in that riding, promised the people ample room for a playground. I do not wish to hold up the committee, but I am more surprised than ever that the minister should rise in his place tonight and say that he sees no relationship between the conservation of moisture in Canada and the preservation of muskeg and timber stands. I would ask him to pause and reflect upon what he has said. Why, every hon. member knows that throughout the dominion we have been studying policies whereby we can develop areas. We have been studying the conservation of moisture and the reforestation of various areas.
Twenty years ago or more, as the member of a county council, I was interested in this very question. We started reforestation and to-day we can see the results. Experiments were carried out on patches of twenty, thirty, fifty and a hundred acres, and there were areas in some districts covering from eight to ten square miles. Here we have an area that is twenty square miles. There is not an hon. member who does not know that, especially in the old province of Ontario, there has been a constant study of schemes that would cost millions for the purpose of damming water so as to avoid floods down through the Belleville district and the Guelph and Galt districts. Reforestation has been taken up more or less as a provincial policy, and every county council in Ontario has interested itself in the subject.
In Saskatchewan, we are told, the proposal under consideration will not affect the area in question. Millions are being spent to conserve moisture in seeding down, because after all, next to trees, there is nothing that will preserve moisture more than grass, and next to muskeg there is nothing that will better serve that purpose than trees. All you have to do is to ride along the highways when the snow disappears and you will see trees, large and small, if they are thick enough, with snow still under them. If one flies over northern Ontario one will see snow up there a month after it has disappeared in the open. Surely no one knows better than the Minister of Agriculture that trees, lakes and rivers are of enormous advantage. I know that what the minister has said is to some extent true, that the rain will fall just the same if these few' trees are cut down. Surely he does not think, however, that they can be taken over to the other part of Saskatchewan. I would suggest to the minister that he read that book prepared by an able industrialist, Mr. Aubrey Davis, and endorsed by every forest ranger, and he will change his mind. He will agree that when trees are cut down, streams and springs dry up.
I can show the minister areas in my own county to illustrate the point I am making. I have one area particularly in mind, and there were a number of small areas of two or three acres. Twenty-five years ago, I understand, there were five or six bubbling springs on that area and the trees were cut off. In later years, when the springs dried up, the agricultural society reforested the area and recently three of the springs have appeared again.
This country needs a national reforestation policy. Years ago I said, both in this house and elsewhere, that if we went on exploiting we w'ould some day regret it-and I do not say that as a reflection on the friends of the
National Parks-Prince Albert

minister. I am speaking of exploitation generally such as we have had through the years, because we have been a nation of exploiters.
We have robbed the forests; we have cleared the ground, rolled back the map until the ground has almost blown away beneath our feet. I am amazed that the minister should suggest that, in a province as dry as Saskatchewan, an area involving almost a quarter of a million acres with all the moisture, and the trees necessary to retain that moisture, is not a permanent asset of that province.
