We are spending a great deal of time on this bill. When the resolution was before the committee I asked the minister how much the saving would be. He did not have the information that night, but my understanding was that he was to have it when the bill came before us. I think we should have that information before this bill is passed. As I recall, the minister said it would mean saving the services of two rangers during the fire-fighting season, which is usually three or four months. The minister should have some information as to the amount spent on fire fighting during the last five or six years. Ten years is a very short time in the life of a park. This park was set aside just a few years ago; I think the first proposal was made in 1926, and the boundaries were defined in 1928. Since then we have had ten years of depression, and the federal government were cautious about appropriations for the development of playgrounds. The minister said this area has not been found necessary for the park, but we should keep in mind the needs of the future, and I can think of no finer asset to this park than a large area of good timber. While there may be a lack of roads through this part of the park, I hope that hon. members sitting here to-night will live long enough to see scenic drives through this Prince Albert national park.
I suggest that the minister let this matter stand until he can give us more information as to the saving to be effected. The last clause of the third paragraph of the explanatory notes reads:
.	. . such lands have a distinct value for
development and settlement.
I agree with the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe as to the need for preservation of forests. For the last ten years we have seen our governments, federal and provincial, and of both parties, setting aside for settlement lands which should have been preserved for park or forest. I know there is a conflict of opinion in the administrative work. Those particularly concerned about forestry have objected to these areas being set aside one after another for land settlement when in their

opinion those areas were much better suited for forests. I have seen Conservative and Liberal governments making appropriations year after year for the settlement of lands, in some instances heavily timbered, to produce more wheat. In 1932 I think it was, when wheat prices were at the lowest levels ever known in the last four hundred years, we still found federal and provincial governments providing money to bring more of these bush lands under cultivation. The federal government has had some responsibility for encouraging the settlement of such lands.
The minister advances, as a reason for taking this area out of the national park, the suggestion that it might have some value for agriculture. With the largest supply of wheat ever on hand in Canada, this government should not be giving away land to be devoted to the production of more wheat and cereals. This park is one of the greatest assets in Saskatchewan. My information is that it is costing very little to retain this area in the park. It should be retained until the minister gives us much more detailed information as to what it is costing the federal treasury. I would ask the minister to consent to have the committee rise and report progress, and to give us further information at a later date.

I should like to say one word in connection with a matter raised earlier in the evening. At another stage of this discussion I suggested that this land originally belonged to the province and that it was only fair it should revert to the province. To support that view, I have before me chapter 41 of the statutes of 1930, which is the Saskatchewan Natural Resources Act. In the schedule to that act there is set forth the memorandum of agreement entered into by the Dominion of Canada and the province of Saskatchewan with regard to the natural resources of that province, in which agreement I find these words:
. . . whereas the government of Canada desires that the province should be placed in a position of equality with the other provinces of confederation with respect to the administration and control of its natural resources as from its entry into confederation in 1905 . . .
Then I omit some lines which are not relevant, and the agreement goes on:
In order that the -province may be in the same position as the original provinces of confederation are in virtue of section one hundred and nine of the British North America Act, 1867, the interest of the crown in all crown lauds, mines, minerals (precious and base) and royalties derived therefrom within the province . . . shall . . . belong to the province .	. . and be administered by the
province for the purposes thereof . . .
Later, it speaks of national parks, and provides that the Prince Albert national park:
.	.	. shall continue to be vested in and
administered by the government of Canada as a national park, but in the event of the parliament of Canada at any time declaring that the said land or any part thereof is no longer required for park purposes, the lands, mines, minerals (precious and base) and the royalties incident thereto, specified in any such declaration, shall forthwith upon the making thereof belong to the province . . .
That makes it quite clear that the intention of this agreement was to put the province of Saskatchewan back to the year 1905 so far as the administration of these natural resources was concerned. Therefore I think it is absolutely correct to say that this land belonged to the province by virtue of this agreement, which was ratified both by this parliament and by the legislature of Saskatchewan. The intent was to put the province of Saskatchewan back to 1905 and to treat these natural resources as though they had belonged to Saskatchewan from that year,

National Parks-Prince Albert
when the province was constituted. I think that is abundantly clear, and this statute, with its particular reference to national parks, bears out that obvious intention.
There is one other point to which I should like to refer. From this discussion the impression might be gathered that it is an abnormal thing to change the boundaries of a park. I do not know what happens elsewhere, but I know that in Nova Scotia, when I had something to do with public affairs there, we took some of our own crown land, bought some other land and gave it all to the dominion for national park purposes. That land was accepted by this government. After a year or two it was found that some of the land had better be taken from the park. I believe on one section there were some fifteen or twenty families, and it was the opinion of the park authorities that this section had better be left out. The boundaries were changed and that land was given back to the province. Where does that agreement lead the minister? It simply leads to this, that in a few isolated instances and with regard to comparatively small areas the boundaries of parks have been changed. But here is an area of some forty square miles being taken right out of a great national park which has been set up for only ten years. When the park was constituted and the boundaries defined, there must have been a long term view taken as to what was going to happen over a period of, say fifty years.
The point is that the minister has not yet made a convincing statement as to why this 
is being done, except on the theory that it will save the wages of two or three fire wardens. We ought to know exactly what is the value of the asset. This land never was the property of the province of Saskatchewan, notwithstanding the declaratory statute to which my hon. friend has referred; but if effect is given to this bill it will become vested in the province, and the natural resources go back as of 1905. That is all the agreement means. A legal position was created there, and the dominion government gave the province of Saskatchewan a grant, after arbitration, in consideration of the alienation of certain of these natural resources.

Yes. I am glad indeed to meet the request of the leader of the opposition, which is a reasonable one. As hon. members are aware, the control of game, the licensing of hunters, permits to trap, and everything relating to the taking of fur-bearing or other wild animals are wholly in the jurisdiction of the provinces within their respective boundaries. A province can take necessary steps to conserve fur-bearing animals within its own boundaries; that is, it can require a trapper to take out a licence to trap, to make a return of his take, and to give any other particulars that the provincial authorities may require of him. The same thing holds true with regard to the shooting of big game, in fact, the taking of any sort of wild animal for any purpose whatsoever.
A rather serious difficulty has, however, arisen in this respect. Frequently wild animals are illegally taken within a province. A province may declare a closed season for a period of time against the trapping or taking of beaver, for example; because, while beaver in large areas have almost disappeared, in our western provinces particularly, and also in the eastern provinces, there was a time in the history of this country when skins taken from beaver constituted a very large part of the total commerce in furs. A province may declare a closed season on beaver, and under those conditions it is illegal for any one to trap or take beaver within that province. As frequently happens, however, some trapper who does not take out a licence, illegally and against the laws of the province traps beaver within the province and has the pelts or skins
Export of Game

for sale. He cannot sell them within the province because, if he attempts to sell within the province, he must produce his licence or permit, and since none was issued to him he is in difficulties. But he will take these pelts or skins across the boundary into another province, and there is nothing in the laws of the second province that prohibits him from making a sale and putting the proceeds in his pocket. The purpose of this bill is to overcome that defect, and it is sought to overcome it by means of proclamation in provinces where it is necessary-and eight out of the nine provinces have asked for it. Then it will be necessary, before the trapper who has taken skins illegally in Saskatchewan, for instance, can sell them in Manitoba, to produce a licence or permit to take them in Saskatchewan. If he is unable to produce a licence or permit showing that he has taken them legally, he is in difficulties in the province in which he tries to sell them. The furs can be seized and he can be charged and fined or, if he fails to pay the fine, imprisoned. That, as simply as I can state it, is the purpose of the legislation.

Yes, to take
them out of the province. But under the law they are allowed to shoot so many, and they must get a permit to ship those birds or game out.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext: That is the jxercise of jurisdiction within a province.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext: Yes, but if they take that game across the boundary, into another province, under the law there is no way of going after them.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext:
It would
be a nusiance in respect of a hunter from Ottawa going to the province of Quebec, and returning with a bag of partridge, a deer or something like that. He would have to have a permit.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext:
They have to
have permits now, in western Canada, to go from one province to another.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext:
The point was raised by
the leader of the opposition as to the power of provincial authorities to regulate movement. The power of those authorities to regulate
movement from one province to another by permit was considered by the Department of Justice. Indeed, this whole legislation was considered, and was approved by the law officers of the crown.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext: I have no doubt about our jurisdiction in interprovincial trade; there is no doubt about that.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext: Does the minister imagine that the provinces will take this up, and institute export permits? They do not all have them now, do they?

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext:
I believe most of them
have. The question of dealing with abuses which have grown up has been under consideration at conferences between the officials of the provinces and of the federal government. Eight of the provinces have asked that legislation of this kind be passed, so that they may effectively control the illegal taking of fur-bearing animals.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext:
It is an
aid in that respect, and good legislation.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext:
The only province which
did not express an opinion in favour was Prince Edward Island. They said they had no objection to it, and stated that the condition did not arise in their province.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext:
They do
not have wild game, anyway.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext:
The game laws of the
provinces are premised upon the fact that the game in the province is owned by the province.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext:
By the
crown.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext:
Yes; and licences are
issued subject to certain terms, namely, that one may shoot so many in a day and so many in a season. If one has an outside licence, such licence contains a permit to export so many. The province has the right to give such privilege, because the crown owns the game. I concede that point, so far as wild game is concerned.
Another point, however, arises when one considers the domesticated fur-bearing animals. I am thinking particularly of Mr. McNeill who runs a fox farm at Fort Qu'Appelle. He has hundreds of foxes which he raises and subsequently kills. He markets their pelts in Montreal and New York, and at one time sold them in London, England. Saskatchewan cannot issue an export licence or forbid anyone so situated from exporting that domesticated furbearing animal, because it does not belong to the crown.
Export of Game

The same question arose in 1920, 1921 and 1922 when there were interprovincial export liquor houses in all the different provinces. Those provinces sought in one way or another to prohibit the export of liquor from one province to another, and were unable so to do. I understand that some years ago in Ontario they either imposed an export duty or forbade the export of pulp logs from the province. That was based on the principle that Ontario or the crown owned the natural resources and timber limits, and that they could authorize the cutting of timber on the understanding that it would not be exported or, if exported, subject only to payment of a certain charge.
Where the definition in section 2, paragraph (b) extends and applies to domestically raised fur-bearing animals, I suggest that the requiring of a licence for an export permit to be issued by the province, as provided in section 3, would be wholly ultra vires.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext: I think the hon. member is right.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext: I would suggest that the section be given further consideration.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext: I understand that in a province a person must obtain a permit from the province to export game. Would that province not be responsible for the punishment of any person breaking the regulation? If this measure passes, would such punishment be placed under the jurisdiction of the dominion, and w-ould punishment of the offender be a federal responsibility?

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext:
As I said earlier, the provinces have complete control over the taking of game and fur-bearing animals within their own boundaries. They do that now, I believe, in every case by the issue of permits or licences to trappers and hunters. But cases have arisen where individuals have taken game and fur-bearing animals illegally, and in the case of the fur-bearing animals have removed the skins from one province to another for purposes of sale. Had they attempted sale within the province where the animals wrere taken, they would have been apprehended, because they could not have produced the necessary permit or licence from provincial game authorities to show that the game had been taken legally.
The purpose of this legislation is not to add to or detract from the powers of provincial governments, but simply to provide machinery to check an abuse.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext: A system of enforcing provincial law.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext: It is the principle of using the added authority of the federal government, so that the provinces may be in a position to enforce their own provincial laws.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext:
Outside their own
provinces. Could they then go outside their own provinces?

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext: No.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext: It may be that the province from which the hon. member comes has a law declaring a closed season for the taking of beaver. No permits would be issued to trap beaver, and any beaver taken would under those circumstances be taken illegally. I know he would not do it, but if the hon. member did trap beaver illegally, and attempted to sell them within the province of Saskatchewan, he would not be able to produce a permit or licence stating that he had a right so to do. But he might slip across to the neighbouring province of Alberta, or into Manitoba. He could show that he was a resident of Saskatchewan and that the beaver skins had not been taken in Manitoba or Alberta. Consequently there would be no machinery to deal with him. This legislation provides the machinery to deal effectively with him.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext:
What about
domestically raised fur-bearing animals which are in an entirely different class from wild animals or birds? Has the province or the dominion the right to regulate the export of such animals between provinces?

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext: I shall have to wralk warily here because I do not belong to the learned profession of the law and must speak as a layman. The province has wide powers in connection with property and civil rights, and I think it would be within the right of a province to go quite far in legislating in connection with matters affecting those rights.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext: But they cannot say that I shall not export my private property, my horse, for example.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext: Let me use an illustration, more to seek knowledge than to impart information. Assume that a farmer has some very fine silver foxes and that he is the only person in the province who has such foxes. The provincial authorities might take note of it and say that for a certain time the progeny of those foxes shall be retained in the province and refuse him the right to export.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext:
They
could not do it.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext:
I shall not attempt to discuss that with my hon. friend. I fall back upon what I said a moment ago, that this legislation has been approved by the law officers of the crown. I assume that if there

Condensed Milk
is anything in the bill along the lines referred to by the hon. member for Regina, it will be made manifest in due course.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext: I think most of us are confused. We can understand the minister's argument with reference to wild game; we realize that it is perfectly logical, but what we cannot understand is how the argument applies to domestic fur-bearing animals. Such animals are in the same position as live stock. They are a farm product, a totally different thing from wild game. Will the minister explain why this wild game legislation is being applied to domestic fur-bearing animals?

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext: I think I can help out the committee. There have been cases of theft of domestically raised furbearing animals and it is to keep down that sort of thing.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext:
Section 3 (a)
states that no person shall knowingly take, carry, and so on, except under the authority of an export permit duly issued under the laws of such province. The province has no right to give a permit in connection with domestically raised fur-bearing animals. Therefore any person who would carry such animals across the border would be in immediate contravention of the law if this bill is passed. The bill says "permit duly issued," but they cannot issue a permit when they have not the right to do so.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext:
Have the provinces
asked to have domestically raised animals included?

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext: I cannot answer that at the moment. It is almost eleven o'clock, and since we are not likely to get through to-night, I shall move that the committee rise and report progress.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF SHIPMENTS OUT OF PROVINCE WITHOUT PROPER PROVINCIAL AUTHORIZATION
speechtext:
Will the minister give consideration to subsection 2 of section 5? It may be all right for a game officer to have jurisdiction anywhere in Canada, but these game officers should not have the powers of a justice of the peace. They are to be the complainant, the prosecutor, the judge, the one who levies the fine and the one who carries it right on. That is very bad legislating. I would refer also to section 10 of the bill. All lawyers know that the criminal code provides that there shall be only one matter of complaint in any one specific charge. This section provides that section 710 of the criminal code shall not apply to any proceedings in respect of any offence under this bill. That is not good practice because that section is in the criminal code for good and important reasons.
I am not going to elaborate upon it, but one offence under one charge is the principle which has been applied in our criminal law. If there are other offences, they are brought forward under separate charges so that the accused is not called upon to meet a dozen cases in one charge. I bring that to the minister's attention.
Progress reported.

Tuesday, April 1, 1941.
